seasonal_care.march: Active growth resuming. Flower stalks emerging.
seasonal_care.april: Bloom — small flowers on branching inflorescences. Bees active.
seasonal_care.may: Nuts from previous blooms developing. Fertilize again.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — fast frond growth. Nut development continuing.
seasonal_care.july: Growth at peak. Monitor nut development — remove mature nuts regularly in high-traffic areas.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — mature coconut palms are moderately hurricane-resistant but dropping nuts are a hazard in storms. Secure or remove nuts before storms.
seasonal_care.september: Nut harvest if desired. Continued growth.
seasonal_care.october: Reduce irrigation. Another bloom cycle possible.
seasonal_care.december: Dry season. Reduce irrigation for established palms.

common_problems.symptoms: Rapid frond yellowing progressing upward, premature nut drop, death
common_problems.solution: Malayan dwarf varieties are resistant to lethal yellowing — the primary reason they are recommended over tall varieties. Tall coconut palms are extremely susceptible. Choose dwarf varieties.

common_problems.symptoms: Coconuts dropping from height
common_problems.solution: Remove maturing nuts regularly, especially near seating and walkways. The Malayan dwarf's lower height makes this more manageable.

common_problems.symptoms: Spear leaf death, rotted growing point
common_problems.solution: Copper fungicide spray on emerging spear. Treat promptly — bud rot can kill quickly.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and some big box garden centers. Always specify Malayan Dwarf for disease resistance and manageable size.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida nurseries — specify Malayan Dwarf
plants.expert_tips: If you plant a coconut palm in SW Florida, plant the Malayan Dwarf (golden or green variety) rather than the traditional tall type. The dwarf stays at 20-30 feet vs 80-100 feet, produces coconuts within 3-4 years vs 6-10 years, is resistant to lethal yellowing disease that kills tall varieties, and has far less falling-nut hazard. Regular fertilization with palm fertilizer is essential — SW Florida's sandy soil cannot sustain a coconut's high nutrient demands without supplementation.
plants.fun_fact: The coconut is the most economically important palm in the world — every part is used. The husk fiber (coir) is used for rope, matting, and growing media. The shell is used for bowls, charcoal, and activated carbon. The water is drunk. The meat is eaten and pressed for oil. The oil is used in cooking, cosmetics, and biofuel. The fronds are woven into thatch, baskets, and mats. The trunk is used for construction. No other single plant provides such a complete range of useful products.
plants.traditional_uses: The coconut palm has no natural wild population — it has been cultivated and spread by humans across the tropical world for over 4,000 years. Polynesian peoples brought it across the Pacific; Arab traders spread it across the Indian Ocean world. In Florida, it arrived with European and Caribbean settlers. Every use described in the fun fact above has deep cultural roots in dozens of civilizations.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental and food plant. No invasive concerns in Florida. Moderate supplemental wildlife value. Lethal yellowing disease has eliminated many traditional tall coconut populations in south Florida.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA rules vary — some communities restrict tall varieties due to falling nut liability. Malayan Dwarf is more widely HOA-approved. Confirm before planting.

plants.description: Not actually a palm at all — a cycad. Extremely popular in SW Florida landscapes for its neat symmetrical form. However it is one of the most dangerously toxic plants to dogs and cats in existence. Virtually no wildlife value.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — one of the most poisonous plants to pets in Florida. All parts are toxic; seeds are extremely dangerous and can cause liver failure and death in dogs and cats. Avoid entirely if pets have yard access.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove only fully dead or dying fronds. Wear gloves — all parts are toxic. Never remove green fronds.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy to grow but the pet toxicity and Asian cycad scale require ongoing vigilance. Consider native Zamia integrifolia as a safer alternative.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: No wildlife value. Highly toxic to pets. Asian cycad scale is a serious ongoing threat. Limited ecological value.
plants.propagation_seed: Not recommended — seeds take 1-3 years to germinate and all parts are highly toxic.
plants.propagation_cutting: Remove offsets (pups) from the base of the mother plant. Allow cut surface to dry 24 hours before planting in well-drained sandy mix.
plants.propagation_division: Removing basal pups is the standard propagation method.
plants.germination_notes: Always propagate from pups. Handle with gloves — all parts are highly toxic.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Very well-drained soil. Drought tolerant once established. Plant with crown at soil level. Handle with gloves — all parts are highly toxic. The seeds (orange-red when mature) are especially dangerous to dogs and children. If you have dogs with access to the yard, seriously consider replacing sago palms with safer alternatives.
do_not_plant_near: Anywhere pets can access — all parts are highly toxic to dogs and cats
Children's play areas — seeds are highly toxic
plants.looks_like_plants: Florida coontie (Zamia integrifolia) — native cycad
plants.looks_like_notes: Florida coontie is the native cycad alternative for SW Florida. Zamia has smaller softer leaflets and stays very low (2-3 feet); sago palm is larger and more robust (3-10 feet). Zamia is pet safe and ecologically valuable as host plant for Atala butterfly — a far superior choice for SW Florida landscapes.
plants.attracts_specific: No significant wildlife attraction — plants that are toxic to most animals generally don't attract wildlife.

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. No irrigation needed. No action needed.
seasonal_care.february: Good month for new frond cycle — flush of new leaves emerges annually.
seasonal_care.march: New frond flush emerging. New leaves are bright green and soft before hardening.
seasonal_care.april: New fronds hardening off. No irrigation needed for established plants.
seasonal_care.may: Established plants completely drought tolerant. No action needed.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season. No action needed.
seasonal_care.july: If planting new specimens, water weekly until established.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — very durable, low to ground.
seasonal_care.december: Dry season. No irrigation needed for established plants.

common_problems.symptoms: White powdery encrustation on all surfaces, yellowing, plant death
common_problems.solution: This devastating invasive scale has killed millions of cycads in Florida. Treat immediately with horticultural oil spray (thorough coverage required) and/or systemic insecticide. Monitor monthly and treat proactively.

common_problems.symptoms: Vomiting, weakness, seizures, jaundice in dogs after ingesting any plant part
common_problems.solution: EMERGENCY VETERINARY CARE IMMEDIATELY — survival rate is low even with treatment. Every minute matters. Sago palm poisoning is the most common cause of fatal plant poisoning in dogs in Florida.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, crown rot, death
common_problems.solution: Excellent drainage is essential. Does not tolerate wet feet.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Consider Zamia integrifolia (Florida coontie) as a native alternative.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: The most important thing about sago palm is the toxicity. It is the most common cause of fatal plant poisoning in dogs in Florida — by a wide margin. The seeds are particularly dangerous but all parts can kill a dog that ingests them. If you have dogs, do not plant sago palm. If you already have sago palms and dogs, consider removing the palms or permanently restricting dog access to those areas. Asian cycad scale is also a serious ongoing threat — inspect monthly and treat immediately at first sign.
plants.fun_fact: Sago palm is not a palm at all — it is a cycad, a completely different ancient plant lineage that predates flowering plants by over 200 million years. Cycads were dominant plants during the Jurassic period and are essentially living fossils. The nearest relatives of cycads are not palms but conifers and ginkgos. The sago palm's palm-like appearance is entirely convergent evolution — it independently evolved a similar growth form.
plants.traditional_uses: Cycas revoluta is native to Japan's southern islands (Ryukyu Islands). In Japan, the starch from the trunk was historically processed as an emergency food (requiring extensive washing to remove the toxins). The plant is deeply associated with Japanese garden culture where it is a traditional element of formal garden design.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental from Japan. Asian cycad scale (Aulacaspis yasumatsui) has devastated cycad populations worldwide including in Florida — monitoring and treatment are essential ongoing responsibilities.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved but widely reconsidered due to pet toxicity awareness. Note Asian cycad scale requirement in maintenance specifications.

plants.description: The king of SW Florida fruit trees. Thrives in Cape Coral's heat and humidity. Grafted trees fruit in 2-3 years. Prune annually after harvest to control size and promote production. Watch for anthracnose fungal disease during wet season.
warnings: Mango sap and skin can cause skin irritation in sensitive people. Mango pit and skin can cause digestive issues in pets — keep pits away from dogs.

varieties.name: Carrie
varieties.notes: One of the best backyard varieties — compact tree, incredibly rich flavor, no fiber. Self-pollinating. Early harvest May-June.

varieties.name: Cogshall
varieties.notes: Top condo mango — slow growing, very easy to control size. Perfect for small yards or containers. Fiberless, excellent flavor.

varieties.name: Nam Doc Mai
varieties.notes: Thai variety with sweet fragrant fiber-free fruit. Semi-dwarf, manageable size. July-August harvest.

varieties.name: Kent
varieties.notes: Considered one of the sweetest Florida mangoes. Large tree but excellent production. Late season harvest July-August.

varieties.name: Keitt
varieties.notes: Best late season variety — stays green when ripe. Large fruit, heat tolerant, excellent disease resistance. Harvest August-September.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None during bloom/fruit set. Weekly for young trees.

plants.pruning_notes: Prune 1/3 of canopy immediately after harvest — this is the most critical management practice for continued production.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy with correct variety selection and post-harvest pruning. SW Florida's climate is genuinely ideal for mango production.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Excellent edible fruit. Critical bee forage during winter bloom. Bird and mammal fruit source. Major supplemental wildlife value during fruiting.
plants.propagation_seed: Polyembryonic varieties produce true-to-type seedlings but take 5-8 years to fruit. Not practical for named varieties.
plants.propagation_cutting: Not commonly done — grafting is standard.
plants.germination_method: Plant fresh seed 1 inch deep in moist sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Always buy grafted trees from reputable nurseries for named varieties and reliable fruit quality.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Well-drained soil. Plant grafted trees for 2-3 year fruit production. Best varieties for SW Florida: 'Cogshall' (compact, good for small yards), 'Julie' (low-fiber, sweet), 'Keitt' (late season, large), 'Nam Doc Mai' (Thai variety, excellent flavor), 'Glenn' (early, reliable). Avoid 'Haden' and 'Tommy Atkins' — these perform poorly in SW Florida's climate.
do_not_plant_near: Power lines — can reach 40+ feet without pruning
Sensitive people — sap causes skin reactions in some individuals
plants.looks_like_plants: Mango varieties look similar to each other — verify variety before purchase
plants.looks_like_notes: Named grafted mango varieties can only be distinguished by fruit characteristics. Buy from reputable tropical fruit nurseries with clearly labeled grafted varieties.
plants.attracts_specific: Northern mockingbird (fruit), Red-bellied woodpecker (fruit), Various parrot species (fruit), Squirrel (fruit), Raccoon (fruit), Honeybee (flowers — critical early-season nectar), Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Dry season stress triggers flower bud development. No irrigation for established trees. Panicles emerging.
seasonal_care.february: Bloom — cream-colored panicles covering the tree. One of the most important bee forage events of the year. No irrigation.
seasonal_care.march: Fruit set. Small green fruits developing. Fungicide spray for anthracnose if wet weather.
seasonal_care.april: Fruits enlarging rapidly. Irrigate young trees weekly. Watch for fruit fly.
seasonal_care.may: Fruit approaching maturity. Harvest when fruit gives slightly to pressure and smells fragrant at the stem end.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — primary harvest for most varieties. Prune immediately after harvest for next year's crop.
seasonal_care.july: Post-harvest pruning critical. Remove 1/3 of canopy to promote fruiting wood and manage size.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Young trees may need staking. Pruned trees recover vigorously.
seasonal_care.september: New vegetative growth from post-harvest pruning. No irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.october: Growth continuing. Reduce irrigation to stress tree slightly for bloom initiation.
seasonal_care.november: Begin withholding irrigation — drought stress promotes flower bud development.
seasonal_care.december: Continued drought stress. Flower buds developing. Do not irrigate.

common_problems.symptoms: Black spots on fruit and flowers, fruit rot, flower blight in wet conditions
common_problems.solution: Copper fungicide spray during bloom and early fruit development. Ensure good air circulation. Choose anthracnose-resistant varieties.

common_problems.symptoms: Damaged seeds inside fruit, exit holes
common_problems.solution: Difficult to control once established. Collect and dispose of fallen fruit. Some variety resistance.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown leaf tips and edges
common_problems.solution: Reduce irrigation. Increase soil organic matter. SW Florida's salt-containing irrigation water accumulates over time — occasional deep flushing helps.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Named grafted varieties available at tropical fruit nurseries. Pine Island Nursery (Miami area) and local CRFG (California Rare Fruit Growers) chapter sales are excellent sources. Avoid unnamed seedling mangoes at big box stores.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at tropical fruit nurseries and some big box garden centers — always buy named grafted varieties
plants.expert_tips: Mango is the quintessential SW Florida fruit tree. Two critical success factors: variety selection and post-harvest pruning. For variety: choose grafted trees of 'Cogshall' for small yards, 'Julie' for best flavor, or 'Keitt' for late-season production. Avoid varieties that are standard at big box stores — many perform poorly in SW Florida's humidity. For production: prune aggressively to 1/3 of the canopy immediately after harvest. This is the most counter-intuitive but most important management practice — the new vegetative flush from post-harvest pruning produces next year's fruit. Skip the pruning and production declines year over year.
plants.fun_fact: Mango has been cultivated in India for over 4,000 years — it appears in Sanskrit texts from 1500 BCE and was a sacred tree in Hindu tradition. Alexander the Great tasted mangoes in India during his conquest (326 BCE). The Mogul Emperor Akbar planted an orchard of 100,000 mango trees. Today mango is the most consumed tropical fruit on earth by weight — over 50 million metric tons per year.
plants.traditional_uses: One of the most important plants in South Asian culture for 4,000+ years — fruit eaten fresh, dried, and pickled; leaves used in Hindu ceremonies; wood used for furniture and tools; bark and leaves used medicinally. Not part of Florida indigenous traditions — introduced by European settlers.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from South Asia. No invasive concerns in Florida. Important supplemental food source for birds and wildlife during fruiting. SW Florida is one of the best climates in the continental US for mango production.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval varies — size and fruit drop are considerations. Compact varieties like 'Cogshall' are more HOA-friendly.

plants.description: Excellent fruit tree for SW Florida in well-drained spots. West Indian varieties are best suited to Cape Coral's heat. Needs good drainage. Plant Type A and Type B varieties together for best pollination. Watch for laurel wilt disease.
warnings: Toxic to pets — the leaves, bark, skin, and pit contain persin which causes vomiting and diarrhea in dogs and cats. Keep fallen fruit picked up.

varieties.name: Choquette
varieties.notes: One of the most popular Florida backyard varieties. Large fruit up to 3 lbs, good flavor. Harvest November-January.

varieties.name: Monroe
varieties.notes: Large high-quality fruit with excellent flavor. Good disease resistance. Pairs well with Choquette for cross-pollination.

varieties.name: Brogdon
varieties.notes: Most cold-tolerant Florida variety. Medium fruit, good flavor. Harvest August-October.

varieties.name: Hall
varieties.notes: Excellent disease resistance — recommended by UF/IFAS. Good flavor, medium-large fruit. Harvest October-November.

varieties.name: Lula
varieties.notes: Classic Florida variety, cold tolerant, good production. Medium fruit with rich flavor. Harvest October-December.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Weekly in dry season — consistent moisture critical during fruit development

plants.pruning_notes: Prune to manage height and canopy after harvest. Open center pruning improves air circulation and fruit production.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Moderate — drainage and laurel wilt monitoring are critical. Correct variety pairing is essential for fruit production.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Edible fruit. Bee pollinator plant. Bird and mammal fruit source. Laurel wilt risk requires vigilance.
plants.propagation_seed: Avocado seeds germinate easily but seedling trees take 7-15 years to fruit and fruit quality is unpredictable. Always buy grafted trees.
plants.propagation_cutting: Not commonly done — grafting is the standard commercial method.
plants.germination_method: Place seed broad end down in water until sprout emerges, then plant.
plants.germination_notes: Always buy grafted trees — seedling trees have unreliable fruit quality and very long juvenile period.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Excellent drainage — avocado roots are extremely sensitive to waterlogging. Well-drained sandy or loamy soil. Plant one Type A and one Type B variety for cross-pollination. Best varieties for SW Florida: 'Monroe' (large, Type B, excellent), 'Choquette' (large, Type A, very good), 'Simmonds' (Type A, good flavor), 'Brogdon' (Type B, cold-hardy for zone 9b). West Indian varieties perform best in SW Florida's heat.
do_not_plant_near: Low-lying areas with poor drainage — root rot is fatal
Near other laurel-family plants if laurel wilt is present in the area
plants.looks_like_plants: Florida avocado varieties look similar to each other — verify Type A/B designation before purchase
plants.looks_like_notes: Type A and B varieties are visually similar — differentiated by flowering behavior, not appearance. Always label trees when planting.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybee (primary pollinator — essential for fruit production), Various bee species, American robin (fallen fruit), Raccoon (fallen fruit)

seasonal_care.january: Cool dry season. Reduce irrigation. No action needed.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month. Fertilize with avocado-specific fertilizer.
seasonal_care.march: Bloom — small yellowish-green flowers. Bees essential for pollination. Type A and B varieties must be planted together.
seasonal_care.april: Fruit set. Small fruits developing. Water regularly.
seasonal_care.may: Fruits enlarging. End of dry season — irrigate regularly.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season. Monitor for laurel wilt — no cure, remove infected trees immediately.
seasonal_care.july: Continued fruit development. Fruit from some varieties beginning to ripen.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Stake young trees. Mature trees are fairly wind-resistant.
seasonal_care.september: Harvest window for some early varieties.
seasonal_care.october: Main harvest for most varieties. Harvest when fruit reaches full size — avocados ripen off the tree.
seasonal_care.december: Reduce irrigation. Good pruning month after harvest.

common_problems.symptoms: Sudden wilting of branches, brown streaking in wood, rapid tree death
common_problems.solution: No cure. Remove and destroy infected trees immediately — do not chip wood or move wood from property. The fungus is spread by the redbay ambrosia beetle. Proactive insecticide trunk injections can protect healthy trees in high-risk areas.

common_problems.problem: Root rot in poorly drained soil
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves, branch dieback, tree decline and death
common_problems.solution: Excellent drainage is non-negotiable. Plant on a slight mound in heavy soil areas. No recovery once Phytophthora root rot is established.

common_problems.symptoms: Small fruits dropping before maturity
common_problems.solution: Inconsistent irrigation during fruit development causes drop. Maintain consistent moisture during fruit sizing.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Named grafted varieties at tropical fruit nurseries. Fruitscapes (SW Florida) and Tropical Acres are good local sources.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at tropical fruit nurseries — buy named grafted varieties only
plants.expert_tips: Avocado requires the best drainage you can provide in SW Florida — the sandy nature of Cape Coral's soil is actually an advantage over clay-heavy sites. Always plant two trees: one Type A (flowers open as female in morning, male in afternoon) and one Type B (flowers open as female in afternoon, male in morning) for cross-pollination. Laurel wilt has devastated avocado orchards in south Florida — know the symptoms and act immediately if you see them.
plants.fun_fact: Avocado has one of the most unusual pollination systems of any cultivated fruit tree — the same tree's flowers function as female on one day and male the next, preventing self-pollination. This is called 'dichogamous' flowering and is why planting a Type A and Type B together is critical — the complementary timing of A (female morning/male afternoon) and B (female afternoon/male morning) ensures overlap in pollination.
plants.traditional_uses: Avocado originated in Mexico and Central America where it was cultivated by the Aztec and Maya for at least 5,000 years. The Aztec called it 'ahuacatl.' It was introduced to Florida by European settlers in the mid-1800s and has been cultivated in south Florida ever since.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Mexico/Central America. Laurel wilt disease poses a significant ongoing threat to avocado production in south Florida — monitor trees carefully.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval generally easy — attractive evergreen tree. Note fruit drop concerns near walkways.

plants.description: One of the best all-around wildlife shrubs for Southwest Florida. Tubular red-orange flowers bloom nearly year-round attracting hummingbirds and butterflies constantly. Dark berries eaten by many bird species. Host plant for the pluto sphinx moth. Important: only plant the true native Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf, African, or compacta varieties.
warnings: Do NOT buy dwarf, African, or compacta varieties — they are not native and have significantly less wildlife value.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None — SW Florida rainfall sufficient once established

plants.growth_notes: Can reach 6 ft in first season under ideal conditions
plants.pruning_notes: Hard prune in spring to maintain size and encourage dense bushy growth
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most forgiving native shrubs in SW Florida. Tolerates poor soil, drought, and neglect.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, supports 5+ wildlife categories, year-round host and nectar source
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe berries, clean pulp, sow fresh. Germination in 14-21 days.
plants.propagation_cutting: Softwood cuttings in spring-summer. Root in moist mix, 3-4 weeks.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates best — viability drops quickly
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants easily from container. Water well for first 2-3 weeks. Avoid transplanting in peak summer heat — fall is ideal in SW Florida.
plants.looks_like_plants: African firebush (Hamelia patens var. glabra), dwarf firebush, compacta firebush
plants.looks_like_notes: Dwarf, African, and compacta varieties look similar but are not native and have significantly less wildlife value. Always verify you are buying Hamelia patens var. patens.
plants.attracts_specific: Pluto sphinx moth (Xylophanes pluto) — host plant; Ruby-throated hummingbird; Gulf fritillary butterfly; Zebra longwing butterfly

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. Enjoy winter blooms.
seasonal_care.february: Good time to prune if size control needed before spring flush.
seasonal_care.march: Apply slow-release fertilizer if desired. New growth begins.
seasonal_care.april: Monitor for whitefly — treat with neem oil if needed.
seasonal_care.may: Peak growing season begins. Water weekly if no rain for 2+ weeks.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season begins — typically no irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.july: Monitor for fungal issues in humid conditions. Remove dead wood.
seasonal_care.august: Continue monitoring. Peak wildlife activity on berries and flowers.
seasonal_care.september: Berries abundant — peak bird attraction. Excellent planting month.
seasonal_care.october: Best time to plant new specimens. Fall planting season begins.
seasonal_care.november: Continue fall planting. Prune lightly if needed.
seasonal_care.december: No action needed. Hardy through SW Florida winters.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing leaves, sticky residue, white insects under leaves
common_problems.solution: Spray with neem oil solution weekly for 3 weeks. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial insects visiting the flowers.

common_problems.symptoms: Long bare stems with foliage only at tips, reduced flowering
common_problems.solution: Hard prune to 12-18 inches in late winter or early spring. Will rebound vigorously with dense bushy growth within 6-8 weeks.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida native plant nurseries. Ensure you buy Hamelia patens var. patens — not dwarf or African variety.
plants.where_to_buy_local: FNPS plant sales, native plant nurseries throughout Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: The single most common mistake with firebush is buying the wrong variety — African and dwarf forms are widely sold but have a fraction of the wildlife value. The true native grows large — plan for 6-8 ft and prune hard once a year rather than clipping constantly. Hummingbirds will find it within days of planting if they are in the area.
plants.fun_fact: Firebush berries contain compounds studied for antimicrobial and antioxidant properties. The Seminole people used the plant medicinally.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally by indigenous peoples of Central and South America. Berries used in traditional beverages in some cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: Populations of the true native firebush are declining in the landscape trade as non-native varieties dominate nursery stock. Buying and planting the true native variety actively supports genetic conservation of the species in SW Florida.
plants.hoa_notes: Many SW Florida HOAs now accept native plants. Lee and Collier County have native plant provisions.

plants.description: Famous for its extraordinary clusters of metallic purple berries eaten by over 40 bird species and deer. Host plant for spring azure butterfly. Low maintenance — dies back and rebounds vigorously each season. Adaptable to sun through shade.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing on new growth each season. Hard annual pruning keeps it productive and compact.
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back hard to 12-18 inches in late winter or early spring annually. This is essential for best berry production — beautyberry blooms and fruits on new growth.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the easiest and most rewarding natives in SW Florida. Adapts to nearly any condition from full sun to deep shade. Annual hard pruning is the only real management task.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Berries eaten by 40+ bird and mammal species. Host plant for spring azure butterfly. Natural insect repellent properties. Exceptional ecological value.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect berries when fully ripe and purple. Clean pulp from seeds, sow in moist sandy mix. Cold stratification not required in SW Florida. Germination is reliable.
plants.propagation_cutting: Easy from softwood cuttings in summer. Take 4-6 inch cuttings, strip lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, keep humid. Roots in 3-4 weeks.
plants.propagation_division: Established clumps can be divided in late winter. Dig and separate rooted stems carefully.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow in moist sandy mix, barely cover.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seeds germinate readily without pretreatment. Cuttings are faster and the preferred method.
plants.transplant_notes: Very easy to transplant. Plant in almost any soil from full sun to full shade. Water weekly for first 3 months. Space 4-6 feet apart for mass planting effect — beautyberry is most spectacular in groups.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns
plants.looks_like_plants: Brazilian beautyberry (Callicarpa dichotoma) — non-native ornamental
plants.looks_like_notes: Brazilian beautyberry has smaller leaves and smaller berry clusters. American beautyberry is larger in all respects and the berry clusters wrap completely around the stem rather than sitting on one side. For SW Florida, if it's growing wild it's almost certainly the native.
plants.attracts_specific: Northern mockingbird, American robin, Gray catbird, Cedar waxwing, Eastern towhee, Brown thrasher, White-eyed vireo, Spring azure butterfly (host plant), Various bees, White-tailed deer

seasonal_care.january: Dry season dormancy. Plant looks scraggly or cut back — this is normal. No irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.february: Good month to cut back hard to 12-18 inches if desired — it will rebound vigorously. Last chance before spring growth.
seasonal_care.march: New growth emerging rapidly. Fertilize lightly with slow-release. No irrigation needed unless newly planted.
seasonal_care.april: Active growth. Leaves expanding. End of dry season — water new plantings deeply.
seasonal_care.may: Fast growth. Small pink-purple flowers beginning to appear. Water new plantings.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Heavy flowering. Bees and butterflies active.
seasonal_care.july: Flowers giving way to green berry clusters. Spectacular berry development begins.
seasonal_care.august: Berries turning metallic purple — one of the most extraordinary sights in SW Florida. Wildlife activity peaks.
seasonal_care.september: Full berry production. Over 40 bird species and deer feeding heavily. Do not prune.
seasonal_care.october: Berry season at peak. Mockingbirds, robins, and cedar waxwings stripping berries.
seasonal_care.november: Berries dwindling. Good month to plant new beautyberry.
seasonal_care.december: Plant winding down for winter. Reduce irrigation. The bare winter form is part of its character.

common_problems.problem: Leaf spot in wet humid conditions
common_problems.symptoms: Brown or gray spots on leaves, premature leaf drop
common_problems.solution: Usually minor and cosmetic. Improve air circulation. Remove heavily affected leaves. Healthy plants outgrow it.

common_problems.symptoms: Bronzed stippled leaves, fine webbing on undersides
common_problems.solution: Strong water spray to undersides of leaves. Insecticidal soap if severe. More common in drought conditions.

common_problems.symptoms: Plant grows well but produces few berries
common_problems.solution: Most common cause is insufficient sun. Move to brighter location or thin overhanging trees. Heavy nitrogen fertilizer also reduces berry production.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Widely available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales. Increasingly available at big box garden centers. Very inexpensive in small sizes — buy several for maximum impact.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida native nurseries, FNPS sales, and increasingly at big box stores
plants.expert_tips: Cut it to the ground every winter or early spring. Seriously — it looks alarming but beautyberry is one of those plants that blooms and fruits best on new growth. Hard annual pruning keeps it compact, vigorous, and producing maximum berries. Left unpruned it gets tall and leggy with sparse berry production.
plants.fun_fact: Beautyberry leaves contain callicarpenal, a natural insect repellent compound. USDA research has shown it to be as effective as DEET against mosquitoes and ticks. Crushing a few leaves and rubbing them on skin is a genuine folk remedy that has scientific backing.
plants.traditional_uses: Seminole and other indigenous peoples used crushed leaves as an insect repellent and bruised roots in baths to treat rheumatism and fever. Leaves were placed in horses' harnesses to repel flies. Berries were used to make jelly.
plants.conservation_notes: Common and secure native throughout SW Florida. An excellent choice for habitat restoration — fast-growing, adaptable, and extraordinarily productive for wildlife. No conservation concerns.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval varies — the winter dormant form looks untidy. Frame as a wildlife habitat plant and demonstrate the spectacular berry season for best results.

plants.description: Widely planted for extraordinary drought and salt tolerance, fast growth, and showy flowers in pink, white, red, and yellow. However the toxicity is severe and demands serious thought before planting in home landscapes with children or pets.
warnings: HIGHLY TOXIC — all parts including sap, flowers, leaves, stems, and water in a vase containing oleander are extremely toxic to humans, pets, horses, and livestock. Smoke from burning branches is toxic. One of the most dangerous common landscape plants.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None — one of the most drought tolerant shrubs available

plants.growth_notes: Fast growing — can reach full size within 2-3 years from a small container plant.
plants.pruning_notes: Prune in late winter or after bloom cycles. Always wear gloves and long sleeves — sap is toxic. Dispose of all prunings in trash. Never compost or burn oleander.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Extremely easy in the right location. Unmatched for coastal, drought, and heat tolerance. The toxicity requires thoughtful siting but is manageable for most landscapes.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Limited native wildlife value due to toxicity. Good nectar source for some insects. Primary value is ornamental and for challenging sites where few plants survive.
plants.propagation_seed: Not commonly used — seeds are viable but variable. Collect seed pods when dry, sow in well-drained mix. Germination is reliable but seedlings may not match parent plant characteristics.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy — the standard method. Take 6-10 inch tip cuttings, allow cut end to dry 24 hours, plant in moist sandy mix. Roots readily in warm weather with or without rooting hormone.
plants.germination_method: Direct sow in well-drained sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds germinate readily. Cuttings from a known variety are preferred to ensure flower color and form.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants easily at almost any size. Full sun essential — plants in shade are leggy and bloom poorly. Well-drained soil required. Extremely salt and drought tolerant once established. Wear gloves when handling — all parts are highly toxic.
do_not_plant_near: Areas accessible to children or unsupervised toddlers
Pet areas
Vegetable gardens — toxic sap contamination risk
Fire pits or fire features — burning is toxic
plants.looks_like_plants: Frangipani (Plumeria spp.) when young — similar long leaves
plants.looks_like_notes: Oleander leaves are long narrow and pointed in whorls of 3; frangipani leaves are larger and clustered at branch tips with milky sap. Oleander has no milky sap. Both are toxic — handle either with care.
plants.attracts_specific: Oleander aphid (year-round colony), Oleander caterpillar / polka-dot wasp moth (Syntomeida epilais), Honeybee (nectar despite toxicity to most insects), Monarch butterfly (nectar)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established plants need no water. Good month to assess structure and prune if needed — wear gloves, never burn prunings.
seasonal_care.february: Good pruning month before spring growth flush. Remove dead or crossing branches. Dispose of all prunings in trash — never compost or burn.
seasonal_care.march: Spring growth flush begins. Fertilize lightly if desired. New growth may show caterpillar feeding — normal.
seasonal_care.april: Active growth. Flower buds forming. No pruning after this point.
seasonal_care.may: Blooming begins. Spectacular flower display. No action needed.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Peak bloom continues through summer.
seasonal_care.july: Continued blooming. Watch for oleander aphids — yellow with black legs, very visible.
seasonal_care.august: Continued bloom. Hurricane month — oleander is very wind resistant.
seasonal_care.september: Bloom continuing. Good month to do light shaping if needed.
seasonal_care.october: Bloom slowing. Reduce irrigation for newly planted specimens.
seasonal_care.november: Good planting month. Blooming may continue in warm years.
seasonal_care.december: Possible light frost protection needed in zone 9b. Established plants handle brief frosts well.

common_problems.symptoms: Clusters of bright yellow aphids with black legs on new growth and flower buds, sticky honeydew, sooty mold
common_problems.solution: Strong water spray dislodges most colonies. Insecticidal soap for persistent infestations. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides — beneficial insects control aphids naturally.

common_problems.symptoms: Distinctive orange and black spiny caterpillars rapidly defoliating branches
common_problems.solution: Handpick on small plants. Bt spray for larger infestations. Plants recover quickly from defoliation. The caterpillar becomes a beautiful polka-dot wasp moth.

common_problems.symptoms: Browning and scorching of leaf edges, progressive dieback, eventual plant death
common_problems.solution: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Do not propagate from infected material. Disease spread by sharpshooter insects.

common_problems.problem: Root rot in poorly drained soil
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, wilting, death from base up
common_problems.solution: Oleander requires well-drained soil — it does not tolerate wet feet. Ensure drainage. No recovery once root rot is established.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Very inexpensive. Many named varieties available — specify flower color when purchasing.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: The toxicity is real and serious — one of the most poisonous common landscape plants. That said, oleander has been planted in SW Florida for a century without widespread incident because it tastes terrible and most children and pets avoid it naturally. The key rules: never burn prunings (smoke is toxic), always wash hands after handling, and do not plant where toddlers or unsupervised children play. In appropriate locations it is genuinely unbeatable for drought, salt, heat, and year-round bloom.
plants.fun_fact: Oleander is so toxic that honey made by bees that forage heavily on oleander flowers can cause illness — a phenomenon documented in ancient times and referenced by Pliny the Elder. Despite this, oleander is the official flower of the city of Hiroshima because it was the first plant to bloom after the atomic bomb was dropped.
plants.traditional_uses: Not native to Florida — Mediterranean origin. Historical medicinal uses in its native range include heart treatments (the cardiac glycosides are medically active but the therapeutic window is extremely narrow and poisoning is easy). Not recommended for any home use.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no invasive concerns in Florida. Xylella fastidiosa (bacterial leaf scorch) has become a serious threat to oleander populations throughout Florida — monitor plants carefully.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved and very commonly used in SW Florida community landscapes. Check HOA rules before removing existing specimens.

plants.description: One of the most essential hummingbird and butterfly plants for Southwest Florida. Brilliant red spikes bloom nearly year-round. Self-seeds prolifically so you will always have more. Very drought tolerant and easy. Excellent companion to firebush and blue porterweed.
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back hard to 6-8 inches 2-3 times per year to maintain compact form and maximum bloom. Allow some plants to self-seed.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the easiest and most rewarding hummingbird plants available. Self-sustaining once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Primary hummingbird plant for SW Florida. Year-round bloom. Self-seeding. Exceptional ecological value.
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds fall and self-sow prolifically — allow some to remain on the ground. Collect and scatter where you want more plants. Sow on surface of moist soil.
plants.propagation_cutting: Tip cuttings in summer root easily in 2-3 weeks.
plants.propagation_division: Established clumps can be divided. Each division needs roots.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow on moist soil — do not bury deeply.
plants.germination_notes: One of the easiest plants to germinate. Self-sows so reliably that you rarely need to intentionally propagate it.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Very drought tolerant once established. Well-drained soil. Space 18-24 inches apart. Allow self-seeding to fill in over time — a colony of scarlet sage maintains itself indefinitely.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns
plants.looks_like_plants: Mexican sage (Salvia leucantha) — similar flower spike form
plants.looks_like_notes: Scarlet sage has brilliant red tubular flowers; Mexican sage has purple and white velvety flowers. Both are excellent hummingbird plants. Scarlet sage is native/near-native; Mexican sage is non-native.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary — visits multiple times daily), Rufous hummingbird (winter migrant), Monarch butterfly, Gulf fritillary, Zebra longwing, Swallowtail butterflies, Bumblebee, Various native bees

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established plants need no water. Red spikes may slow slightly but blooming continues.
seasonal_care.february: Good month for hard cutback to 6-8 inches to rejuvenate. New bloom flush follows in 3-4 weeks.
seasonal_care.march: New vigorous growth. Heavy bloom. Hummingbirds arriving with spring migration.
seasonal_care.april: Peak spring bloom. Hummingbirds and butterflies constant. No action needed.
seasonal_care.may: Heavy bloom continues. Self-seeding beginning — seedlings appearing around the parent plant.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Vigorous growth and bloom. Cut back lightly if getting too tall.
seasonal_care.july: Heavy summer bloom. The most important hummingbird plant in SW Florida in summer.
seasonal_care.august: Continued bloom. Hurricane month — flexible stems handle wind well.
seasonal_care.september: Continued bloom. Seedlings establishing for next season.
seasonal_care.november: Best planting month. Bloom continues year-round.
seasonal_care.december: Bloom continues. Dry season — established plants need no water.

common_problems.symptoms: White insects on leaf undersides, yellowing
common_problems.solution: Strong water spray on leaf undersides. Insecticidal soap if severe.

common_problems.symptoms: Tall spindly stems with few leaves and flowers
common_problems.solution: Cut back hard to 6-8 inches. New compact growth with heavy bloom follows quickly.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Very widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Often sells out during hummingbird season — buy in fall or early spring.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Scarlet sage is arguably the single most important hummingbird plant available for SW Florida — it self-seeds prolifically, blooms year-round, requires essentially no care, and produces exactly the red tubular flowers that hummingbirds evolved to visit. Once established in your garden it will reproduce indefinitely. Let the seedlings grow wherever they appear and within a few years you will have a self-sustaining colony.
plants.fun_fact: Scarlet sage is native to the Americas including the southeastern US and is classified as native or near-native in Florida depending on the authority — its range extends into Florida naturally, though it has also been widely spread by cultivation. This ambiguity makes it one of the 'gray area' natives that most Florida native plant experts accept as functionally native for habitat purposes.
plants.traditional_uses: Various Salvia species have been used medicinally by Florida indigenous peoples. The Seminole used preparations from related sages for fever and respiratory conditions. The genus Salvia takes its name from the Latin word for 'to heal' — reflecting the long history of medicinal use across many cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: Native or near-native in Florida. An important component of disturbed edge and garden habitats for hummingbirds and pollinators. Self-seeding habit means it can establish in natural areas nearby — not a concern ecologically but worth noting.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved. Year-round red bloom is high-impact for community landscapes.

plants.description: Florida's single best lawn-substitute groundcover. Host plant for common buckeye, phaon crescent, and white peacock butterflies. Tiny white-purple flowers attract native bees constantly. Seeds eaten by birds. Can be mowed. Handles light foot traffic. One of the most ecologically valuable plants per square foot in all of Southwest Florida.
plants.pruning_notes: Mow at 2-inch height every 4-6 weeks if desired for tidiness. Not required — frogfruit looks attractive unmowed at 4-6 inches.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the easiest and most ecologically valuable groundcovers available. Essentially zero maintenance once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Host plant for three butterfly species. Bird seed source. Native bee forage. Florida Friendly lawn alternative. Maximum ecological value for minimum effort.
plants.propagation_seed: Self-seeds prolifically. Collect seed heads when dry and scatter where desired.
plants.propagation_cutting: Stem cuttings root wherever they contact moist soil — the plant's natural spreading mechanism. Press stems into moist soil and they root in 1-2 weeks.
plants.propagation_division: Dig established mats and divide. Each piece with roots establishes readily.
plants.germination_notes: Self-seeds and spreads so readily that active propagation is rarely needed.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Sandy or any well-drained to moderately wet soil. Plant plugs 12-18 inches apart and they fill in within 1-2 seasons. Handles light foot traffic. Can be mowed at 2-inch height every 4-6 weeks. No fertilizer needed. No irrigation once established.
do_not_plant_near: Heavy foot traffic areas — handles light traffic only
plants.looks_like_plants: Creeping Charlie (Phyla nodiflora is sometimes confused with invasive Phyla canescens)
plants.looks_like_notes: Native frogfruit (Phyla nodiflora) and the near-invasive Phyla canescens are very similar — both form low creeping mats with tiny flowers. P. nodiflora has slightly larger flower heads and is native; P. canescens is non-native and can be more aggressive. Buy from reputable native plant sources to ensure correct species.
plants.attracts_specific: Common buckeye butterfly (primary host plant), Phaon crescent butterfly (host plant), White peacock butterfly (host plant), Various native bee species, Honeybee, Eastern towhee (seeds), Mourning dove (seeds)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established mats need no irrigation. Bloom continues year-round. Butterflies active even in winter.
seasonal_care.february: Good month to plant plugs into lawn areas. No irrigation needed once established.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous spring growth. Heavy bloom. Buckeye and crescent butterflies active.
seasonal_care.april: Peak spring bloom and butterfly activity. Can be mowed to 1-2 inches if desired.
seasonal_care.may: Continued growth and bloom. Self-spreads rapidly by rooting stems.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — extremely fast spread. Mow if needed for tidiness.
seasonal_care.july: Heavy summer bloom and butterfly activity. No irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — very low growing and virtually undamaged by wind.
seasonal_care.september: Continued bloom. Good month to plant plugs in patchy areas.
seasonal_care.october: Bloom continues. Reduce any supplemental irrigation.
seasonal_care.december: Bloom continues. Dry season — established plants need no water.

common_problems.symptoms: Mat becomes thin and bare in high-traffic areas
common_problems.solution: Frogfruit handles light occasional foot traffic but not constant heavy use. Use on low-traffic paths and border areas rather than main pathways.

common_problems.symptoms: Spreading into areas where it's not wanted
common_problems.solution: Edge regularly to contain. The spreading habit is the plant's strength — plan its placement accordingly.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales as plugs. Increasingly available at some big box garden centers as lawn-alternative awareness grows.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales
plants.expert_tips: Frogfruit is the single best ecological upgrade you can make to a conventional lawn in SW Florida. It tolerates mowing, handles drought and salt, requires zero fertilizer, supports three butterfly species as a caterpillar host, feeds birds with seeds, and provides nectar for native bees — all while eliminating the fertilizer and pesticide inputs of a conventional lawn. Even replacing 20% of a lawn with frogfruit dramatically increases the ecological value of the property.
plants.fun_fact: Frogfruit gets its unusual common name from its historical use in low-lying wet areas near ponds and streams where frogs are common — the plant's ability to tolerate periodic wet conditions and its typical habitat alongside water bodies led to the 'frog' association. It has also been called 'Turkey tangle fogfruit' in older literature, a name that makes even less sense etymologically.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Seminole peoples inhabited the coastal and wetland habitats where frogfruit is common. The plant was part of the native ground layer community of those habitats. Specific documented traditional uses are limited in published literature.
plants.conservation_notes: Native throughout coastal and disturbed habitats of Florida. One of the highest-value ecological groundcovers available for SW Florida lawns and landscapes. Host plant for three butterfly species. UF/IFAS Florida Friendly Landscaping top-recommended lawn alternative.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval varies — some HOAs restrict non-grass groundcovers. Present as Florida Friendly Landscaping certified lawn alternative with butterfly garden documentation.

plants.description: One of the absolute best native vines for Southwest Florida. Tubular red and orange flowers bloom nearly year-round and hummingbirds are completely unable to resist them. Red berries eaten by birds. Well-behaved unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle. A must-have for any hummingbird garden.
plants.pruning_notes: Light pruning after bloom cycles to shape. Remove dead wood. Does not require heavy pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy. Year-round hummingbird magnet with essentially zero maintenance once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Year-round hummingbird plant. Berry crop for birds. Native vine well-behaved on supports. One of the best native vines available.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe red berries, remove pulp, cold stratify 30 days, sow in moist mix.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy — semi-hardwood cuttings in summer root in 3-4 weeks with rooting hormone.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratify 30 days, then surface sow in moist mix.
plants.germination_notes: Cuttings are faster and more reliable than seed propagation.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Well-drained soil. Very drought tolerant once established. Needs a support structure — fence, trellis, pergola, or shrub. Unlike invasive Japanese honeysuckle, coral honeysuckle does not spread aggressively. Space 8-10 feet apart on a support. Water weekly for first 3 months.
do_not_plant_near: Shaded areas where bloom will be sparse
plants.looks_like_plants: Japanese honeysuckle (Lonicera japonica) — same genus, invasive
plants.looks_like_notes: Coral honeysuckle has tubular red-orange flowers with no fragrance; invasive Japanese honeysuckle has white to yellow fragrant flowers. Coral honeysuckle does NOT twine aggressively and does not spread by underground runners — completely different growth behavior from its invasive cousin.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary — shaped for hummingbird pollination), Rufous hummingbird (winter migrant), American robin (berries), Gray catbird (berries), Hummingbird clearwing moth (nectar), Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. No irrigation needed. Bloom continues year-round. Hummingbirds visiting.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month. No action needed.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous spring growth. Heavy bloom. Ruby-throated hummingbirds arriving.
seasonal_care.april: Peak spring bloom. Extraordinary hummingbird activity. Red berries forming from previous blooms.
seasonal_care.may: Continued bloom. Red berries attracting birds. End of dry season.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Continued bloom.
seasonal_care.july: Heavy summer bloom. Hummingbirds visiting constantly.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — train onto sturdy support. Flexible stems handle wind well.
seasonal_care.september: Continued bloom. Red berry clusters attracting warblers and other birds during fall migration.
seasonal_care.october: Bloom continues. Important fall migration nectar source.
seasonal_care.december: Bloom continues. Dry season — established plants need no water.

common_problems.symptoms: Clusters of soft-bodied insects on shoot tips, curled leaves, sticky honeydew
common_problems.solution: Strong water spray. Insecticidal soap if severe. Coral honeysuckle is more aphid-resistant than Japanese honeysuckle but can have infestations.

common_problems.symptoms: Vigorous growth with few flowers
common_problems.solution: Increase light. Coral honeysuckle blooms best in full to partial sun. At least 4 hours direct sun daily for reliable bloom.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales. Increasingly available at big box garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales
plants.expert_tips: Coral honeysuckle is one of the very best native vines for SW Florida hummingbird gardens — it blooms virtually year-round producing exactly the tubular red-orange flowers that hummingbirds prefer, and unlike its invasive Japanese honeysuckle cousin it is completely well-behaved and won't overtake a garden. Plant it on a fence or trellis near a window or outdoor seating area where you can watch hummingbirds visit multiple times daily.
plants.fun_fact: Coral honeysuckle flowers are shaped specifically for hummingbird pollination — the tube length and diameter match the ruby-throated hummingbird's bill almost exactly. This co-evolution between flower and pollinator has been occurring for millions of years. Bees can access the nectar but are not efficient pollinators; hummingbirds are the primary intended visitor.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to eastern North America including Florida. Seminole and other southeastern peoples used various honeysuckle preparations medicinally — bark and leaf preparations for fever, headache, and as an anti-inflammatory. The berries were recognized as not edible.
plants.conservation_notes: Native throughout eastern North America. An important hummingbird plant throughout its range. Increasingly planted as a wildlife-friendly alternative to invasive Japanese honeysuckle.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved on fences and trellises. Year-round bloom and hummingbird habitat value.

plants.description: One of the most beloved native grasses in Florida. In fall the clouds of airy pink-purple flower plumes are absolutely stunning — glowing in late afternoon light. Seeds eaten by birds. Dense clumps provide cover for ground birds and lizards. Plant in drifts for maximum impact.

plants.description: The single most recommended native aquatic plant for Southwest Florida's canals, ponds, and wet areas. Vivid violet-blue flower spikes bloom nearly year-round. Bees and butterflies visit constantly. Seeds eaten by ducks and water birds. Dense colonies provide critical fish habitat. Edible — seeds eaten like buckwheat, young leaves cooked like spinach.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Permanent water or saturated soil required

plants.growth_notes: Spreads readily by rhizomes to form dense beneficial colonies
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back to water level in late winter if needed to control spread. Division is easy and creates new plants.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the most reliable and easy aquatic natives for SW Florida. Plant it in shallow water or saturated soil and it does the rest.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, year-round bloomer, supports bees, butterflies, birds, fish habitat, edible, and canal-bank stabilizer
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed heads when brown. Direct sow in wet soil or shallow water.
plants.propagation_cutting: Division of rhizomes in spring or fall. Each division with roots will establish quickly.
plants.propagation_division: Easy — divide clumps in spring. Most practical propagation method.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds need consistently wet conditions to germinate. Division is easier and faster.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant rhizomes or divisions directly into wet soil or shallow water up to 12 inches deep. No special care needed — simply keep roots wet.
plants.looks_like_plants: Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes)
plants.looks_like_notes: Water hyacinth is invasive and looks superficially similar when not in bloom. Pickerelweed has a lance-shaped leaf with a heart-shaped base; water hyacinth has rounded inflated leaf stalks. Never plant water hyacinth.
plants.attracts_specific: Wood duck (seeds), Anhinga (nesting cover), Purple gallinule (nesting and foraging), Native bees including bumble bees, Long-tailed skipper butterfly

seasonal_care.january: No action needed. May die back slightly in coolest weather — will rebound.
seasonal_care.february: Division and replanting can be done now if needed.
seasonal_care.march: Growth resumes strongly. Good time to divide and spread.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — thriving conditions.
seasonal_care.september: Seed heads forming — important bird food source.
seasonal_care.november: Good time to divide and replant.
seasonal_care.december: May slow slightly but typically evergreen in SW Florida.

common_problems.symptoms: Distorted new growth, sticky residue, clusters of small insects on stems
common_problems.solution: Strong spray of water knocks them off. Natural predators like lady beetles usually control them without intervention. Neem oil if persistent.

common_problems.symptoms: Expanding beyond intended planting area
common_problems.solution: Division and removal of outer rhizomes in spring or fall. Rhizomes are easy to pull. Regular division also creates plants to share or expand elsewhere.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and aquatic plant specialists throughout SW Florida. Occasionally at big box garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: FNPS plant sales, aquatic nurseries in Lee and Collier counties
plants.expert_tips: Plant pickerelweed in masses rather than as individual specimens — a dense colony of 10-20 plants along a canal bank does far more ecological work than a single specimen. The combination of pickerelweed, duck potato, and alligator flag creates a complete native aquatic edge that stabilizes the bank, filters runoff, and supports a full range of wildlife.
plants.fun_fact: Pickerelweed flowers are trimorphic — the species produces three different flower forms with different arrangements of stamens and pistils to encourage cross-pollination between plants. This is rare in the plant world.
plants.traditional_uses: Young leaf stalks and seeds were eaten by Native Americans. Seeds can be eaten raw or roasted and ground into flour. Young leaves are edible cooked like spinach.
plants.conservation_notes: Pickerelweed colonies along SW Florida's canals provide critical water filtration, removing excess nutrients from runoff before they enter larger water bodies. Replacing invasive aquatic plants with pickerelweed actively improves water quality throughout the canal system.

plants.description: The most iconic epiphyte of the American South. Not a moss, not a parasite — a true flowering bromeliad. Critical nesting material for northern parulas, Baltimore orioles, and other birds. Indicator of clean air quality. Harmless to healthy trees. A living symbol of authentic Florida.
warnings: Spanish moss often harbors chiggers and redbugs — wear long sleeves and gloves when handling fresh fallen clumps.

plants.description: Florida's largest native terrestrial fern — bold arching fronds can reach 6-8 ft creating a dramatic tropical statement. Excellent groundcover under trees and in shaded areas. warnings: Do NOT confuse with invasive tuberous sword fern (N. cordifolia) or Asian sword fern (N. brownii). Native giant sword fern has double-toothed pinnae margins and no tubers on runners. Always verify scientific name at purchase.

plants.description: One of Southwest Florida's most magical native plants — white to pink lily flowers appear seemingly overnight after summer rains. plants.description: The single most destructive invasive plant in Southwest Florida. Forms impenetrable dense thickets that completely displace native vegetation. Red berries look attractive but are mildly toxic and the tree provides almost no native wildlife value compared to the habitat it destroys. Now covers over 700,000 acres in South Florida. Remove immediately whenever found.
warnings: Sap causes severe skin and eye irritation — related to poison ivy. Wear gloves, eye protection, and long sleeves when handling. Berries toxic to pets. Smoke from burning is toxic.
plants.removal_method: Cut stems at ground level and immediately apply concentrated herbicide (triclopyr or glyphosate) to cut surface. DO NOT burn — smoke is toxic. Repeat treatments needed. Root system must be killed or it resprouts. Contact Lee or Collier County Extension for assistance.
plants.growth_notes: Extremely fast growing — can form dense thickets within 2-3 years if not immediately controlled
plants.pruning_notes: DO NOT PRUNE — cutting without immediately treating cut surface with herbicide causes vigorous resprouting
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Grows easily in any condition — this is part of why it is so destructive as an invasive.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Category 1 invasive. No native wildlife value. Actively destroys native habitat.
plants.propagation_seed: N/A — do not propagate
plants.germination_notes: Self-seeds prolifically — birds spread seeds throughout natural areas
plants.transplant_notes: DO NOT TRANSPLANT — invasive species. Remove and destroy all plants.
do_not_plant_near: This IS the plant to avoid — remove from property immediately
plants.looks_like_plants: Florida holly (common name used for this plant), Christmas berry
plants.looks_like_notes: Often sold under misleading common names like 'Florida holly.' The compound leaves with a distinctive turpentine smell when crushed, red berries in dense clusters, and rough gray bark are identifying features. If you smell turpentine when you crush a leaf — it is Brazilian pepper. Remove it.
plants.attracts_specific: Birds eat the berries and spread seeds into natural areas — this is how it spreads so effectively. The wildlife value does not offset the ecological damage.

common_problems.symptoms: Vigorous new growth from cut stumps and roots within weeks of removal
common_problems.solution: Cut must be immediately treated with concentrated triclopyr or glyphosate applied directly to the cut surface within 60 seconds of cutting. Untreated cuts resprout more vigorously than before.

common_problems.problem: Skin and eye irritation during removal
common_problems.symptoms: Redness, burning, swelling from contact with sap
common_problems.solution: Wear gloves, long sleeves, eye protection, and closed shoes during all removal work. Wash exposed skin immediately with soap and water. Related to poison ivy — some people have severe reactions.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: DO NOT PURCHASE. Illegal to plant in Florida. If seen for sale, report to Florida Department of Agriculture.
plants.where_to_buy_local: N/A
plants.expert_tips: The most important thing to know: never cut Brazilian pepper without immediately treating the stump. A cut stump without herbicide will resprout 3-5 new stems for every one you cut — making the problem worse. Always have your herbicide ready before you make the first cut. Small seedlings under 12 inches can be pulled by hand — the root system is shallow when young.
plants.fun_fact: Brazilian pepper is related to cashew, mango, and poison ivy — all members of the Anacardiaceae family. This is why the sap causes skin irritation similar to poison ivy in sensitive individuals.
plants.traditional_uses: Used as a folk remedy in South America for various ailments — however the allergenic properties make self-treatment dangerous. Not recommended under any circumstances.
plants.conservation_notes: Brazilian pepper now covers over 700,000 acres of South Florida — more than any other invasive plant in the state. It costs Florida millions of dollars per year to control. Every plant removed from a private property directly contributes to protecting what remains of SW Florida's native ecosystems.

plants.description: Australian tree that has invaded over 500,000 acres of South Florida's wetlands. Drains wetlands by transpiring enormous amounts of water, converting sawgrass marshes and cypress swamps into melaleuca monocultures. Federally listed noxious weed. Remove immediately.
warnings: Do not burn standing melaleuca — heat triggers seed release from the canopy. One tree can release millions of seeds when burned.
plants.removal_method: Cut and immediately treat stump with concentrated herbicide. Hack and squirt method effective on larger trees. Biological control (Melaleuca snout beetle) available — contact SFWMD for current programs.

plants.description: Free-floating plant from South America that can double its population in two weeks, completely choking canals, ponds, and waterways. Reduces oxygen in water killing fish. Blocks boat traffic. Has infested Florida waterways since the 1880s and costs the state millions annually to control. Never introduce to water features.
warnings: Removal requires permits for aquatic herbicide use in Florida waterways. Contact SFWMD before applying any chemical treatment to canals.
plants.removal_method: Physical removal by hand or equipment for small infestations. Aquatic herbicides (2,4-D, glyphosate labeled for aquatic use) for larger infestations — requires permits. Contact SFWMD for assistance with canal infestations.
