plants.description: Underused native understory tree related to blueberry. Delicate bell-shaped white spring flowers feed bees. Shiny blue-black fall berries attract birds. Bark flakes to reveal attractive reddish layers. Well adapted to Florida's sandy soils.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing understory tree
plants.pruning_notes: Light shaping only. Does not require regular pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Requires acidic sandy soil — fails in alkaline conditions common in SW Florida. Test soil before planting.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bee forage, bird berries, attractive bark
plants.propagation_seed: Collect berries when ripe. Clean and sow in acidic sandy mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow in acidic sandy mix — pH critical
plants.germination_notes: Needs acidic conditions for germination. Alkaline water inhibits germination.
plants.transplant_notes: Requires acidic well-drained sandy soil. Amend planting hole with sulfur and peat to lower pH. Test soil pH before planting. Mulch with pine bark.
do_not_plant_near: Alkaline soil areas without pH amendment
plants.looks_like_plants: Blueberry (Vaccinium corymbosum)
plants.looks_like_notes: Sparkleberry has smaller leaves and more tree-like growth habit than blueberry. The distinctive flaking reddish bark on older specimens is identifying. Berries are smaller and less flavorful than cultivated blueberry.
plants.attracts_specific: Various thrushes (berries), Eastern bluebird (berries), Native bees (spring flowers)

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.february: Flowering begins — small white bell-shaped flowers
seasonal_care.june: Berries ripening dark

common_problems.symptoms: Yellow leaves, stunted growth
common_problems.solution: Almost always caused by soil pH too high. Sparkleberry requires acidic soil (4.5-6.5). Apply sulfur to lower pH and use acidifying fertilizer. This is the most common reason sparkleberry fails in SW Florida landscapes.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Requires acidic soil — confirm your site is appropriate before purchasing.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Sparkleberry is rarely planted but genuinely beautiful especially in older specimens with their distinctive flaking reddish bark. The spring flowers are delicate and beautiful, the fall berries attract birds, and the bark provides year-round interest. Worth the extra effort of soil preparation.
plants.fun_fact: Sparkleberry is in the same genus as blueberries, huckleberries, and cranberries. The berries are edible but extremely astringent — they are essentially left to wildlife, which suits them perfectly.
plants.traditional_uses: Berries used in folk medicine as an astringent. Wood used for small tool handles by some Native American peoples.
plants.conservation_notes: One of the few native acid-soil plants of SW Florida's scrub and flatwood habitats. These ecosystems are among the most threatened in the state.

plants.description: Native coastal hammock tree with clusters of small grape-like fruits beloved by white-crowned pigeons and mockingbirds. Edible for humans — small and tart. Very salt and drought tolerant.
plants.growth_notes: Moderate growth. Slower than sea grape.
plants.pruning_notes: Can be maintained as a specimen tree or large shrub.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in coastal SW Florida. Extremely salt and drought tolerant.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bird food critical for white-crowned pigeons, mammals, coastal habitat
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe purple berries. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed much better than dried.
plants.transplant_notes: Very easy to transplant. Tolerates coastal exposure well.
plants.looks_like_plants: Sea grape (Coccoloba uvifera)
plants.looks_like_notes: Pigeon plum has smaller, narrower leaves than sea grape. The bark is rougher and more textured. Smaller growth habit. Fruit clusters are similar but smaller.
plants.attracts_specific: White-crowned pigeon (primary consumer — critical food source), Mockingbird, Raccoon

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries. Less common than sea grape.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Pigeon plum is specifically named for the white-crowned pigeon — a beautiful bird that has experienced significant population declines as its coastal hammock food sources have been reduced by development. Planting pigeon plum is a direct conservation action for this species.
plants.fun_fact: White-crowned pigeons, which depend heavily on pigeon plum fruit, fly up to 100 miles daily between their nesting grounds in the Florida Keys and feeding areas on the mainland. Each pigeon plum planted in SW Florida is a potential refueling stop on this remarkable daily journey.
plants.traditional_uses: Fruit edible for humans — tart and small but palatable. Used in jams in some Caribbean cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: White-crowned pigeon populations have declined significantly with the loss of coastal hammock habitat. Pigeon plum is one of their most important food sources.

plants.description: Attractive native hammock tree with glossy pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits that many birds eat. Fast-growing and good for quick canopy. Interesting compound leaves give a tropical appearance.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing native hammock tree
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning. Remove dead wood only.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Fast growing and low maintenance in well-drained sites.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, bird and mammal food from fruits, fast canopy establishment
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe purple-black fruits. Clean and sow fresh.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed germinates readily.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Fast growing once established.
plants.looks_like_plants: Other tropical trees
plants.looks_like_notes: The compound pinnate leaves and clusters of small purple-black fruits on reddish stalks are identifying. Attractive tropical appearance year-round.
plants.attracts_specific: Migratory warblers (fruit), Northern mockingbird, Various frugivorous birds

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at select native plant nurseries. Worth seeking out for fast canopy establishment.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Paradise tree is one of the best native trees for quickly establishing a canopy in a restoration planting or new landscape. Its fast growth combined with genuine wildlife value makes it an excellent choice when immediate results are needed.
plants.fun_fact: The seeds of Simarouba glauca contain 55-70% oil and have been researched extensively as a biodiesel crop in tropical regions. The oil quality rivals olive oil for cooking.
plants.traditional_uses: Seeds are pressed for edible oil in Central America and India. The oil is also used medicinally and for soap making.
plants.conservation_notes: A tree of tropical hammocks increasingly rare in SW Florida due to habitat loss.

plants.description: Often overlooked but highly valuable native coastal hammock tree. Small red fruits are an important food source for migrating warblers and vireos. One of the few native trees that tolerates shade well. Very salt tolerant.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing coastal hammock tree
plants.pruning_notes: Minimal pruning needed. Tolerates shaping.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Excellent once established but slow growing and specific to well-drained sites.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native, migratory bird fruit, nesting, shade tolerant — rare trait in coastal natives
plants.propagation_seed: Collect red fruits when soft. Clean and sow fresh in well-drained mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh cleaned seed in sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seed performs much better than stored.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants reasonably well from container. Plant in well-drained site. Tolerates partial shade — unusual for coastal species.
plants.looks_like_plants: Nothing closely similar
plants.looks_like_notes: Blolly identified by its small oval leaves, reddish new growth, and bright red berry clusters attractive to birds. The shade tolerance distinguishes it from most coastal natives.
plants.attracts_specific: Migratory warblers (red berries critical during fall migration), Red-bellied woodpecker, Gray catbird

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth
seasonal_care.august: Berries ripening — peak migrant bird activity

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at select native plant nurseries. Often overlooked but highly recommended by Lee County Extension.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Blolly is specifically recommended by the Lee County Extension as an underused native for coastal SW Florida landscapes. Its shade tolerance makes it invaluable for planting in the understory of larger coastal trees.
plants.fun_fact: Blolly is listed as a 'bird magnet' by the Florida Ornithological Society during fall migration. The red berries ripen precisely when migratory warblers and other migrants are moving through SW Florida.
plants.traditional_uses: Limited documented traditional uses.
plants.conservation_notes: A declining component of SW Florida's coastal hammock habitat. Each planted specimen contributes to preserving this tree in the landscape.

plants.description: Enormously productive in SW Florida. Leaves, pods, seeds, and flowers all edible and highly nutritious. Grows extremely fast. Straight trunks useful as garden stakes. Prune hard regularly to keep productive and manageable.
warnings: Leaves typically eaten cooked or dried rather than raw in large quantities.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Weekly during dry season — reduce in rainy season

plants.pruning_notes: Prune aggressively and regularly — cut back to 3-4 feet every 2-3 months to maintain a productive bushy form. The more you prune the more it produces.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Extremely easy and fast in SW Florida. Regular pruning is the only real management task. Perfect drainage is non-negotiable.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good hummingbird and bee nectar source. Excellent edible landscape value. Limited native wildlife value.

plants.description: Breathtaking tree with clouds of lavender-purple tubular flowers in spring. Feathery fern-like foliage attractive even when not in bloom. Less salt tolerant so better for inland properties. Not invasive in FL.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing ornamental tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead or crossing branches. The feathery canopy is the ornamental feature.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in inland SW Florida in well-drained soil. Salt sensitive — inland sites only.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and butterfly forage from flowers, attractive seasonal ornamental
plants.propagation_seed: Collect flat winged seeds from pods. Sow fresh in well-drained mix.
plants.germination_method: Sow fresh seed in well-drained sandy mix
plants.germination_notes: Germination generally good with fresh seed.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well when young. Plant inland — not salt tolerant. Full sun required.
do_not_plant_near: Coastal and beachfront properties — not salt tolerant
plants.looks_like_plants: Blue jacaranda (same species — only one commonly planted)
plants.looks_like_notes: Jacaranda is unmistakable when in bloom — clouds of lavender-purple flowers before the leaves emerge. The feathery bipinnate leaves are also distinctive.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees (flowers), Native bees, Butterflies

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth — full leaf canopy

common_problems.symptoms: Good leaf growth but few or no flowers
common_problems.solution: Jacaranda flowers best with a pronounced dry period. SW Florida's dry season usually provides this. Overwatering or irrigating through the dry season can reduce flowering. Reduce or eliminate irrigation November-February.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Jacaranda flowers before its leaves emerge in spring — the entire tree appears covered in purple before a single leaf is visible. Plant it where you can see the full canopy effect, ideally with morning light behind it.
plants.fun_fact: Jacaranda is considered one of the world's most beautiful flowering trees and appears in countless famous cityscapes including Pretoria South Africa, Buenos Aires Argentina, and Lisbon Portugal.
plants.traditional_uses: The bark of jacaranda has been used medicinally in South American traditional medicine. No significant food uses.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no significant invasive concerns in SW Florida.

plants.description: One of the most commonly planted shade trees in SW Florida. Dense evergreen canopy provides excellent shade and bird nesting habitat. Very hurricane resistant. Salt and drought tolerant. Slow growing but extremely long-lived.
plants.growth_notes: Slow growing but extremely long-lived
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead wood. Strong natural form requires no shaping.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very low maintenance. Slow growth is its primary limitation.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bird nesting and food, dense shade canopy
plants.propagation_seed: Not commonly propagated from seed. Usually purchased as container grown stock.
plants.germination_notes: Not typically grown from seed in home landscape context.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well from container. Very drought and salt tolerant once established. Slow to establish.
do_not_plant_near: Areas where its eventual large size would be a problem — slow growing but gets very large
plants.looks_like_plants: True olive tree (Olea europaea)
plants.looks_like_notes: Black olive is not an olive tree at all — no olives. The common name comes from the small olive-like fruits. The dense evergreen canopy and strong branch structure are distinctive.
plants.attracts_specific: Various birds (nesting in dense canopy), Small birds (insect foraging)

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Very widely available at SW Florida nurseries and garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Black olive is one of the most reliable large shade trees for SW Florida — extremely hurricane resistant, salt tolerant, and long-lived. The slow growth is frustrating but the eventual result is one of the most dependable large canopy trees available.
plants.fun_fact: Despite the common name, black olive (Bucida buceras) is completely unrelated to the true olive (Olea europaea) and produces no edible fruit. The name came from the vaguely olive-like appearance of its small fruits.
plants.traditional_uses: The dense hard wood is used for construction and furniture in its native range in the Caribbean and Central America.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native but widely used and not considered invasive in SW Florida.

plants.description: Stunning ornamental with large velvety deep purple flowers and soft fuzzy leaves. Bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds visit frequently. Not salt tolerant — better for inland properties.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing ornamental. Can become large quickly.
plants.pruning_notes: Prune after flowering flushes to maintain size and encourage reblooming. Hard prune tolerant.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Requires slightly acidic soil — struggles in SW Florida's alkaline substrate without amendment. Also cold sensitive.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee butterfly and hummingbird forage, stunning ornamental
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds rarely practical. Softwood cuttings preferred.
plants.propagation_cutting: Softwood cuttings root readily in spring-summer.
plants.germination_notes: Cuttings are the standard propagation method.
plants.transplant_notes: Plant in acidic amended soil. Full to partial sun. Inland sites preferred. Cold sensitive — protect if temps drop below 35F.
do_not_plant_near: Coastal salt-spray areas — not salt tolerant. Alkaline soil without amendment.
plants.looks_like_plants: Nothing closely similar
plants.looks_like_notes: The large velvety deep purple flowers with prominent stamens and soft fuzzy leaves are distinctive and unmistakable.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees, Bumblebees, Butterflies, Hummingbirds

seasonal_care.january: No action needed in SW Florida
seasonal_care.june: Continued blooming in rainy season
seasonal_care.december: Blooming continues in mild SW FL winters

common_problems.symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis, poor growth
common_problems.solution: Usually iron deficiency from alkaline soil. Apply chelated iron and sulfur to lower soil pH. Use acidifying fertilizer. This is the primary challenge of growing tibouchina in SW Florida.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and garden centers.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Tibouchina needs slightly acidic soil to perform at its best in SW Florida — if yours is turning yellow, the soil pH is too high. Apply sulfur and chelated iron as a rescue treatment, then switch to an acidifying fertilizer for ongoing maintenance.
plants.fun_fact: Tibouchina flowers contain a natural purple dye that has been used in traditional textile dyeing in South America.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally in Brazilian folk medicine for various conditions. Bark extracts studied for antimicrobial properties.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no significant invasive concerns in SW Florida.

plants.description: Spectacular tree cascading with long hanging clusters of bright yellow flowers in spring. Bees and butterflies visit the flowers actively. Birds eat the seeds.
warnings: Toxic to pets and livestock — all parts especially seed pods are toxic. The pulp is used medicinally but should never be self-administered.
plants.growth_notes: Fast growing spectacular flowering tree
plants.pruning_notes: Prune only dead wood. The weeping branch habit is the ornamental feature.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in SW Florida's heat with good drainage. Drought tolerant once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Non-native, bee and butterfly forage, bird seed, beautiful seasonal ornamental
plants.propagation_seed: Collect long brown seed pods when mature. Seeds need scarification. Sow in warm well-drained mix.
plants.germination_notes: Scarify seed coat with file or soak in hot water 24hr.
plants.transplant_notes: Transplants well when young. Full sun required. Excellent drainage essential.
do_not_plant_near: Pet and livestock areas — all parts including pods are toxic
plants.looks_like_plants: Other Cassia/Senna species
plants.looks_like_notes: Golden shower tree identified by its spectacular pendulous clusters of pure yellow flowers and very long (1-2 ft) cylindrical dark brown seed pods. Unmistakable when in bloom.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybees (flowers), Cloudless sulphur butterfly (larval host for related species), Birds (seeds)

seasonal_care.january: No action needed
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season growth

common_problems.problem: Toxic seed pods accessible to pets
common_problems.symptoms: Pet illness after ingesting pods or seeds
common_problems.solution: Remove fallen seed pods promptly from areas accessible to pets. Keep dogs away from fallen pods. The pods look like potential chew toys to dogs — a genuine risk.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Not documented
plants.expert_tips: Golden shower tree puts on one of the most spectacular flower displays available in SW Florida — cascading yellow clusters so dense the flowers can obscure the foliage entirely. For maximum impact, site it where you can see it from inside your home during its spring bloom.
plants.fun_fact: Golden shower tree is the national tree of Thailand and is used in Thai New Year celebrations. The flowers appear on Thai national documents and symbols.
plants.traditional_uses: The pulp inside the seed pods is used medicinally as a laxative throughout tropical Asia. Used in Ayurvedic medicine for thousands of years. The wood is used for furniture and small carved items.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native but widely planted ornamental. The African tulip tree (a serious invasive) is sometimes confused with flowering trees like golden shower — always verify species before planting.

plants.description: Distinctive multi-trunk clumping native palm of the Everglades and SW Florida wetlands. Small black fruits eaten by birds and small mammals. Dense clumps provide excellent nesting and shelter. Tolerates periodic flooding well — excellent for low spots and canal edges.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None — rainfall sufficient; tolerates both wet and dry

plants.pruning_notes: Remove only fully dead fronds. The natural clumping form with reddish basal matting is part of the plant's distinctive character — do not over-clean.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in wet to moderately wet conditions. One of the most distinctive and ecologically valuable native palms for SW Florida wetland landscapes.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Critical Everglades wetland species. Nesting habitat for wading birds. Fruit source for wildlife. Authentic SW Florida native landscape plant.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe black fruits. Remove pulp and sow fresh seeds immediately in moist sandy mix. Germination moderately reliable.
plants.propagation_division: Separate offsets from established clumps with roots attached. Best done in fall.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Division of established clumps is faster and more reliable than seed propagation.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Tolerates wet conditions and periodic flooding — excellent for low-lying areas, canal banks, and rain gardens. Also tolerates moderate drought once established. Plant in groups for best visual impact and wildlife habitat value.
do_not_plant_near: Very dry upland areas without irrigation plan
plants.looks_like_plants: No close lookalikes — the clumping multi-trunk fan palm form with reddish matting is distinctive
plants.looks_like_notes: The multi-trunk clumping habit with distinctive reddish-brown fiber matting at the base and fan-shaped fronds is diagnostic. No other common SW Florida palm has the same form.
plants.attracts_specific: Great blue heron (potential nesting), White ibis, Snowy egret, Northern mockingbird (fruits), Gray catbird (fruits), Raccoon (fruits), Bees (flowers)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established clumps need no irrigation. Dense clumps provide excellent winter bird cover.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month near water features.
seasonal_care.march: New fronds emerging. Small flower stalks forming.
seasonal_care.april: Bloom — small yellow flowers on drooping stalks. Bees active.
seasonal_care.may: Fruits developing from flowers. End of dry season.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — fast frond growth. Tolerates seasonal flooding well.
seasonal_care.july: Fruits developing from green to orange to black. Dense growth providing nesting cover.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — clumping multi-trunk form is very wind-resistant.
seasonal_care.september: Fruit season continuing. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.october: Berries feeding birds and small mammals.
seasonal_care.december: Dry season. Dense clumps provide excellent winter wildlife cover.

common_problems.symptoms: White or brown crusty bumps on fronds and stems
common_problems.solution: Horticultural oil spray in cooler months. Healthy established plants tolerate moderate infestations.

common_problems.symptoms: Little visible growth in first year
common_problems.solution: Normal — paurotis palm invests in root development. Keep consistently moist for first year and resist the urge to assume failure.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries specializing in SW Florida and Everglades species. FNPS chapter sales and SFWMD giveaways are good sources.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales
plants.expert_tips: Paurotis palm is one of the most distinctively Floridian palms available — its clumping multi-trunk form with reddish-brown matting at the base and fan-shaped blue-green fronds is immediately recognizable as 'Florida Everglades.' It is the defining palm of the Big Cypress and Everglades wetland margins. For SW Florida properties with pond edges, canal banks, or wet low spots, paurotis palm provides both an authentic sense of place and exceptional wildlife habitat in the dense clumps.
plants.fun_fact: Paurotis palm clumps are one of the most important nesting sites for wading birds in the Everglades — great blue herons, wood storks, anhingas, and white ibis all nest in the dense paurotis clumps found throughout Big Cypress and the Everglades. The multi-trunk structure with interwoven fronds creates a platform that rivals mangroves for colonial wading bird nesting.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa and Seminole peoples built their culture around the Everglades and Big Cypress wetlands where paurotis palm is a dominant species. Fronds were used for thatching and weaving. The dense clumps provided habitat for the fish, birds, and game that sustained these civilizations.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to the Everglades, Big Cypress, and coastal wetlands of SW Florida. Critical wetland habitat species. Threatened by hydrological changes and development throughout its range. Planting paurotis palm in wet landscape areas directly contributes to wetland habitat restoration.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for waterfront properties. Distinctive form provides authentic Florida landscape character.

plants.description: Elegant native fan palm with a slender trunk and graceful crown. Small white fruits eaten by birds. Very salt and drought tolerant. Fragrant flowers attract bees.
warnings: Threatened species — purchase only from reputable nurseries growing legally propagated specimens.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove only dead fronds. Self-cleaning in good conditions. Minimal pruning needed.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy but slow. Patience and appropriate siting in full sun coastal conditions are the keys.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Threatened native species. Coastal habitat plant. Bird fruit source. Bee forage. Elegant landscape value.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe white fruits. Remove pulp, sow seeds fresh in moist sandy mix. Germination moderately reliable.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seeds germinate better than stored. Buy nursery-grown plants for practical establishment.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Sandy, well-drained, coastal soil. Highly salt tolerant — excellent for beachfront and coastal properties. Drought tolerant once established. Slow growing — buy the largest nursery specimen you can afford for reasonable establishment time.
do_not_plant_near: Shaded areas — needs full sun
Wet areas — requires excellent drainage

plants.looks_like_notes: Florida thatch palm has fan fronds with silvery-white undersides; Key thatch palm has more uniform green fronds; Florida silver palm has strongly two-toned silver undersides. All three are similar elegant native coastal fan palms.
plants.attracts_specific: Northern mockingbird (fruits), Gray catbird (fruits), Various bee species (fragrant flowers)

common_problems.symptoms: Rapid frond bronzing and death
common_problems.solution: No cure. Remove infected plants. Florida thatch palm is susceptible — monitor closely.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries specializing in south Florida species. Buy nursery-grown only — wild collection of this threatened species is illegal.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at specialty native plant nurseries
plants.expert_tips: Florida thatch palm is one of the most elegant native palms for coastal SW Florida landscapes — slender, graceful, salt-tolerant, and genuinely wild-looking in the best possible sense. The fragrant flowers are a bee draw and the small white fruits are bird food. The main challenge is patience — this palm grows slowly. Buy the largest container specimen you can find and afford.
plants.fun_fact: Florida thatch palm is one of only a handful of palms native to the United States and is found naturally only in the Florida Keys and extreme southern Florida. It is the characteristic palm of the Florida Keys hammock and coastal ecosystems — the same habitats that are among the most threatened on earth due to sea level rise and development.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Tequesta peoples used thatch palm fronds for roofing — the name 'thatch palm' directly references this use. The strong fronds were also woven into mats and baskets. The tree was a primary building material for indigenous coastal settlements.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to the Florida Keys and extreme southern Florida — threatened by habitat loss and sea level rise. Listed as threatened in Florida. Only nursery-grown plants should be purchased. Planting in landscape settings throughout SW Florida helps maintain the species in cultivation.

plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for coastal landscapes. Elegant native form is distinctive and appropriate for coastal community landscaping.

plants.description: The world's most cold-hardy palm — native to Florida. Low clumping growth with vicious needle-like spines makes it impenetrable cover for ground-nesting birds. Shade tolerant — one of very few palms that grows well in partial to full shade.
warnings: Extremely sharp needle-like spines can cause serious injury to people and pets. Plant away from foot traffic and pet areas.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Occasional irrigation in dry season — shade reduces drying

plants.pruning_notes: Remove only dead fronds — with extreme care. Heavy leather gloves and eye protection mandatory. The spines cause serious injury.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in shade — one of very few palms that thrives in full shade. Extremely slow growing. Essentially indestructible once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Shade-tolerant native palm. Impenetrable nesting and shelter habitat. World's most cold-hardy palm. Unique ecological role.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe orange-brown fruits. Remove pulp and sow seeds immediately in moist well-drained mix. Germination is very slow.
plants.propagation_division: Remove offsets from established clumps carefully — avoiding the sharp needle spines. Wear heavy leather gloves and eye protection.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist mix.
plants.germination_notes: Very slow germination. Division of established clumps is more practical. Buy container-grown plants.
plants.transplant_notes: Partial to full shade — one of the very few palms that thrives in shade. Moderate moisture. Excellent in shaded understory situations under live oaks where most palms fail. Handle with extreme care — the long black needle spines cause serious puncture wounds. Wear leather gloves and eye protection when planting or pruning.
do_not_plant_near: Foot traffic areas — spines cause serious injury
Pet areas — spines penetrate paws and skin
Children's play areas
plants.looks_like_plants: Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) — both are low native clumping palms
plants.looks_like_notes: Needle palm has very long (6-12 inch) black needle spines at the base of each frond and a more upright trunk; saw palmetto has shorter serrated frond stems and a lower spreading habit. The dramatic black needle spines of Rhapidophyllum are unmistakable.
plants.attracts_specific: Eastern towhee (nesting in impenetrable spiny clumps), Carolina wren, Opossum (shelter), Raccoon (shelter), Ground-nesting birds

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. No irrigation needed. Dense growth provides winter wildlife cover.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month. No action needed.
seasonal_care.march: New fronds emerging. Slow but steady growth.

seasonal_care.july: Continued slow growth. Dense clump provides excellent ground-level shelter.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — very dense low form and flexible fronds make this extremely hurricane-resistant.

common_problems.symptoms: Deep puncture wounds from the needle spines
common_problems.solution: Always wear heavy leather gloves and eye protection when working near or with needle palm. Treat puncture wounds promptly — palm spines can introduce infection.

common_problems.symptoms: Minimal visible progress year to year
common_problems.solution: Normal — needle palm is one of the slowest-growing native palms. Completely normal. Patience.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales. Less common at big box stores. Worth seeking for shaded native landscape plantings.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS chapter sales
plants.expert_tips: Needle palm is the world's most cold-hardy palm — it has survived temperatures of -5°F (-21°C) in experiments. In SW Florida this cold hardiness is irrelevant, but it means the plant is essentially indestructible in our climate. The impenetrable spiny clumps are legendary for providing safe nesting and denning sites for ground-nesting birds, rabbits, and small mammals — nothing can reach the animals sheltering inside a mature needle palm clump. Plant it where nothing else will grow under large shade trees.
plants.fun_fact: The needle palm's cold tolerance record — surviving -5°F in a controlled experiment and regular documented outdoor survival at 0°F — makes it the most cold-hardy palm in existence. Palm enthusiasts have grown it in New York City, Chicago, and even southern Canada. In those locations it's a novelty. In SW Florida it's simply a tough, valuable native landscape plant that happens to have an extraordinary superpower it never needs to use.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Seminole peoples lived alongside needle palms in the shaded hammock habitats. The extremely sharp spines made the clumps useful natural barriers — settlements were sometimes sited near dense needle palm thickets for defensive purposes. Fronds were used for thatching and weaving.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to the southeastern US including Florida, where it inhabits shaded hammock understories. An important component of the native understory palm community. The vicious spines provide irreplaceable secure denning and nesting habitat for ground-dwelling wildlife.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval varies — the vicious spines may concern some HOAs. Best sited in back corners away from foot traffic. The wildlife habitat value is excellent.

plants.description: One of the most popular privacy screening palms in SW Florida. Clumping multi-stem growth creates a dense lush hedge quickly. Birds nest in the dense fronds and eat the small fruits. Requires regular fertilization in FL's sandy soils.
warnings: Listed as caution for invasive potential in South Florida by UF/IFAS — plant where fruit drop can be managed.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove dead or yellowing stems at the base. Do not over-prune — maintain dense clump for privacy screening. Apply palm fertilizer rather than pruning to address yellowing.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy with regular fertilization. SW Florida's sandy soil requires supplemental palm fertilizer for best appearance.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Minimal wildlife value. Excellent privacy screening value. Regular fertilization required.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe yellow to orange fruits. Remove pulp and sow seeds immediately in moist sandy mix.
plants.propagation_division: Divide established clumps — separate stems with roots in fall. Moderately easy.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Division of established clumps is faster and more reliable for privacy screening applications.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Well-drained soil. Regular fertilization essential in SW Florida's sandy soil — areca palms are heavy feeders and show deficiency symptoms (yellowing) without supplementation. Space 3-5 feet for screening hedge. Water weekly for first year.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns beyond fertilization management
plants.looks_like_plants: Bamboo palm (Chamaedorea seifrizii) — similar clumping multi-stem form
plants.looks_like_notes: Areca palm has feathery pinnate fronds and golden-yellow cane-like stems; bamboo palm has similar feathery fronds but darker green stems. Both are used for screening. Areca palm grows larger and faster.
plants.attracts_specific: Northern mockingbird (fruits), Various small bird species (nesting in dense fronds), American robin (occasional fruits)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established clumps need minimal irrigation. Dense fronds provide winter bird shelter.
seasonal_care.february: Good month to fertilize with palm fertilizer. No irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.march: New growth emerging. Good time to remove dead fronds.
seasonal_care.may: Growth accelerating. Fruits developing from previous bloom.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — fast growth. Stop supplemental irrigation.

seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — dense clumping form handles wind well.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing of older fronds, orange-yellow discoloration, frond death
common_problems.solution: Apply palm fertilizer with potassium and magnesium (8-2-12 plus micronutrients formula is standard SW Florida recommendation). Apply 3-4 times per year.

common_problems.symptoms: White shelf fungus at stem bases, stem decline and death
common_problems.solution: Remove infected stems. No cure — the fungus is a soil-borne pathogen. Avoid wounding the stems during mowing. Do not replant palms in infected soil.

common_problems.symptoms: White cottony masses or brown bumps on fronds and stems
common_problems.solution: Horticultural oil spray. Systemic insecticide for severe infestations.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. One of the most commonly sold landscape palms. Available in a wide range of sizes.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Areca palm is SW Florida's most popular privacy screening palm for good reason — nothing else creates a lush dense tropical screen as quickly and as inexpensively. The main management requirement is fertilization: areca palms show potassium deficiency in SW Florida's sandy soil without regular palm fertilizer applications. Apply a palm-specific fertilizer (8-2-12 formula with micronutrients) at least three times per year and the yellow fronds that plague neglected specimens will be a non-issue.
plants.fun_fact: Areca palm is native to Madagascar, where it grows in moist rainforest understories — a very different environment from the dry sandy soil of SW Florida. Despite this, it has adapted remarkably well to Florida's conditions and has become one of the most widely planted landscape palms in the world. The name 'areca' comes from a Malayalam word for a different palm species, the betel nut palm, which Dypsis lutescens superficially resembles.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Madagascar — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Widely cultivated as an ornamental throughout the tropics.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Madagascar. UF/IFAS notes potential for naturalization in disturbed areas in south Florida — plant where fruit drop can be managed. No invasive listing as of current assessment but monitor for spread.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: One of the most commonly specified privacy screening palms in SW Florida HOA landscapes. Include fertilization requirements in maintenance specifications.

plants.description: One of the most popular ornamental palms in SW Florida. Compact, clean, self-cleaning, and produces clusters of vivid red fruits in December. No nutrient deficiency issues that plague queen and foxtail palms. Excellent for smaller yards.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Weekly for first year then minimal

plants.pruning_notes: Self-cleaning — old fronds fall on their own. Remove fallen debris only. No active pruning normally needed.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the easiest ornamental palms for SW Florida. Self-cleaning and compact with spectacular seasonal fruit display.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good bird fruit source. December fruit display is spectacular. Self-cleaning reduces maintenance. No fertilizer problems.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe red fruits. Remove pulp and sow seeds immediately in moist sandy mix. Moderately reliable germination.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seeds germinate better. Buy nursery-grown plants — adonidia is widely available and inexpensive.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Well-drained soil. More drought tolerant and adaptable than most ornamental palms. Self-cleaning — old fronds and fruit clusters fall cleanly without manual removal. Space 6-8 feet for paired or grouped planting. Excellent for small yards due to compact final size.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns
plants.looks_like_plants: Pigmy date palm (Phoenix roebelenii) — both are compact ornamental palms
plants.looks_like_notes: Christmas palm has fan-clean self-cleaning single trunk with green crownshaft; pigmy date palm has feathery pinnate fronds and spiny leaf bases. Christmas palm grows taller (20-25 ft) and is more upright; pigmy date palm stays lower and is more graceful.
plants.attracts_specific: Northern mockingbird (fruits), Red-bellied woodpecker (fruits), American robin (fruits), Various small bird species

seasonal_care.january: Red fruits at their peak — the Christmas display. No irrigation needed. Birds feeding on fruits.
seasonal_care.february: Fruit season ending. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.march: New fronds emerging. Fertilize with palm fertilizer.
seasonal_care.april: Active growth. Flower stalks beginning to emerge from below the crownshaft.
seasonal_care.may: Bloom — small fragrant flowers. Bees active. Fruits from previous season falling.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season. Fruits developing from green to yellow to red.
seasonal_care.july: Fruits turning from yellow to red in late summer.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — self-cleaning and moderately hurricane-resistant.

seasonal_care.october: Fruit season at peak — the Christmas effect building.
seasonal_care.november: Peak red fruit clusters — the plant's most spectacular display. Best planting month.
seasonal_care.december: Vivid red fruit clusters at full peak. Holiday season landmark plant.

common_problems.symptoms: Rapid frond bronzing and death
common_problems.solution: No cure. Remove infected palms. Adonidia is susceptible to lethal bronzing.

common_problems.symptoms: White shelf fungus at trunk base, decline
common_problems.solution: No cure. Remove infected palm. Avoid wounding trunk during maintenance.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Often sold in pairs or multiples for symmetrical plantings.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Christmas palm is one of the most practically useful ornamental palms for SW Florida because it solves problems that plague other ornamental palms. It is self-cleaning (no frond trimming needed), compact (appropriate for most yards), and produces spectacular red fruits in December without the chronic nutrient deficiency issues that afflict queen and foxtail palms. If you want a clean, low-maintenance ornamental palm for a normal-sized yard, this is the one.
plants.fun_fact: Christmas palm is native to the Philippines, where it is called 'Manila palm' — it has no connection to Christmas in its native range. The common name 'Christmas palm' was invented by Florida nursery industry marketing in the 1970s to highlight the timing of the red fruit clusters. The marketing worked spectacularly — it became one of the most popular ornamental palms in the American subtropics.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to the Philippines — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Used ornamentally in tropical Asia for centuries.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental from the Philippines. No invasive concerns in Florida. Moderate wildlife value for bird fruit consumption.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: One of the most HOA-approved ornamental palms in SW Florida. Self-cleaning, compact, and the Christmas fruit display is universally appreciated.

plants.description: Visually striking palm with distinctive plume-like fronds. Very popular in SW Florida despite being poorly adapted to local conditions. Prone to chronic nutrient deficiency in sandy coastal soils. Not salt tolerant.
warnings: Toxic to pets — fruits, fronds, and bark contain toxic compounds. Keep pets away from fallen fruits. Also poorly suited to SW Florida's coastal sandy soils — prone to nutrient deficiency and decline.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove only dead fronds — never over-prune. Never remove green fronds. The frond scar pattern on the trunk is part of the palm's ornamental appeal.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Moderate-high difficulty in SW Florida due to chronic nutrient deficiency. Quarterly fertilization with manganese supplementation is mandatory for success.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Moderate bird fruit value. Pet toxicity concern. High maintenance requirements for acceptable appearance in SW Florida conditions.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe red-orange fruits. Remove pulp and sow fresh seeds in moist sandy mix. Moderately reliable germination.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist sandy mix.
plants.germination_notes: Seeds lose viability quickly — plant within weeks of harvest.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun only. Well-drained soil. NOT salt tolerant — do not plant in coastal salt-spray locations. Regular fertilization is non-negotiable in SW Florida's sandy soil. This palm chronically deficient in manganese, potassium, and boron in local conditions.
do_not_plant_near: Coastal salt-spray areas — not salt tolerant
Pet areas — fruits are toxic to pets
Locations without committed fertilization program
plants.looks_like_plants: Queen palm (Syagrus romanzoffiana) — both have feathery fronds
plants.looks_like_notes: Foxtail palm has distinctive 'foxtail' fronds where the leaflets emerge in multiple directions creating a plume effect; queen palm has flat pinnate fronds. The foxtail's multi-directional leaflets are diagnostic.
plants.attracts_specific: Northern mockingbird (fruits), Red-bellied woodpecker, Various bird species (fruits — but keep pets away)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Nutrient deficiency symptoms often most visible in winter — yellowing fronds.
seasonal_care.february: Apply palm fertilizer with extra potassium and manganese. Critical maintenance month.
seasonal_care.march: New fronds emerging. Apply fertilizer again.
seasonal_care.may: Growth continuing. Fruits from previous bloom developing.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season. Fast growth. Continue fertilizing schedule.
seasonal_care.july: Fruits ripening to orange-red. Birds feeding — but keep pets away from fallen fruits.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — foxtail palm handles wind moderately well.

common_problems.symptoms: Frizzle top — new fronds emerge stunted, frizzled, and yellow-streaked; severe cases cause death
common_problems.solution: Apply manganese sulfate spray directly to emerging fronds and soil application. Critical in SW Florida's alkaline soil. Once frizzle top appears in the spear leaf, the plant rarely recovers fully.

common_problems.symptoms: Oldest fronds yellowing from tips inward, eventually dying
common_problems.solution: Apply palm fertilizer with high potassium (8-2-12 formula) 3-4 times per year. SW Florida's sandy soil is chronically potassium-deficient.

common_problems.symptoms: Vomiting, lethargy, neurological symptoms in dogs or cats after eating fallen fruits
common_problems.solution: Remove fallen fruits immediately in pet-accessible areas. Keep pets away from the tree when fruiting.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Very widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. One of the most commonly sold ornamental palms despite its management challenges.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Foxtail palm is one of the most popular palms in SW Florida despite being poorly suited to local conditions. The chronic nutrient deficiency issues in SW Florida's sandy alkaline soil mean that foxtail palms require a committed quarterly fertilization program to look their best. Without regular manganese applications, frizzle top — a disfiguring and often fatal condition — is almost inevitable. If you want a visually similar palm without the management challenges, consider Royal Palm (Roystonea regia) or Adonidia merrillii instead.
plants.fun_fact: Foxtail palm was one of the last major palm species to be scientifically described — it wasn't formally named until 1978 when an Aboriginal Australian named Wodyeti drew a botanist's attention to it growing in a remote area of Queensland, Australia. The genus name Wodyetia is named in honor of Wodyeti's assistance. The species was essentially unknown to Western science until then, though it is native to a small area of northeastern Australia.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Queensland, Australia — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Extremely recently discovered — essentially no traditional use documentation outside Aboriginal Australian knowledge.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Australia. Foxtail palm requires significantly more resources (water, fertilizer, maintenance) than native alternatives. Consider whether the management commitment justifies the ornamental value vs. better-adapted alternatives.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Widely used in SW Florida HOA landscapes but frequently shows nutrient deficiency. Include mandatory quarterly palm fertilization in HOA maintenance contracts.

plants.description: One of the most rewarding fruit trees for SW Florida — the climate here is genuinely ideal. Needs a slightly cool dry winter to trigger flowering. Not salt tolerant — avoid coastal beachfront sites. Slow to start but very long-lived and productive.
warnings: Lychee seeds and unripe fruit contain hypoglycin-like compounds toxic to pets. Keep pets away from fallen fruit and seeds.

varieties.name: Mauritius
varieties.notes: The most widely recommended and reliable lychee for Florida. Consistent producer, good flavor, bright red fruit.

varieties.name: Brewster
varieties.notes: Large attractive fruit, very heavy producer in good years.

varieties.name: Sweetheart
varieties.notes: Small seed means more edible flesh. Excellent sweet flavor.

varieties.name: Emperor
varieties.notes: Newer variety producing very large fruit. Growing in popularity.

plants.pruning_notes: Light pruning after harvest. Open canopy for air circulation. Never prune heavily before bloom season.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Moderate — winter drought stress management is essential. SW Florida's climate is ideal when correctly managed.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Excellent edible fruit. Critical bee forage during bloom. Bird fruit source. One of the best tropical fruits for SW Florida.
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds lose viability within days and seedlings take 10-25 years to fruit. Never propagate from seed.
plants.propagation_cutting: Air-layering is the standard propagation method for lychee — produces fruiting trees in 1-2 years.
plants.germination_method: Not recommended — always buy air-layered or grafted trees.
plants.germination_notes: Always buy air-layered or grafted trees for reliable fruit production.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Well-drained slightly acidic soil (pH 5.5-7.0). Not salt tolerant — avoid coastal beachfront locations. Requires a cool dry winter — SW Florida's climate is genuinely ideal for this requirement. Best varieties for SW Florida: 'Brewster' (pink-red, reliable), 'Mauritius' (excellent flavor), 'Sweet Cliff' (very sweet, large). Always buy air-layered trees.
do_not_plant_near: Salt-spray coastal areas
Low-lying wet areas
plants.looks_like_plants: Longan (Dimocarpus longan) — similar tree form and fruit
plants.looks_like_notes: Lychee has slightly larger, more vivid red fruits with a bumpy skin; longan has smaller, smoother, tan-brown fruits. Both are in the same family with very similar growing requirements.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybee (flowers — major commercial honey crop in China and SE Asia), Various bee species (fragrant flowers), Red-bellied woodpecker (fruit), American robin (fruit), Various bird species (fruit)

seasonal_care.january: Cool dry weather triggers flower bud development. No irrigation. The cool dry winter is critical for bloom.
seasonal_care.february: Bloom — fragrant white flower panicles appearing. Extraordinary bee activity.
seasonal_care.march: Fruit set. Small green fruits developing. Water regularly.
seasonal_care.april: Fruits enlarging rapidly. Maintain consistent irrigation.
seasonal_care.may: Fruits ripening from green to pink-red. Primary harvest season.
seasonal_care.june: Late harvest in some years. Rainy season begins — stop supplemental irrigation.
seasonal_care.july: Post-harvest care. Prune lightly after harvest.
seasonal_care.november: Continue reducing irrigation — drought stress for flower bud initiation.
seasonal_care.december: Drought stress period — NO irrigation. Critical for next bloom cycle.

common_problems.problem: Failure to bloom without winter stress
common_problems.symptoms: Healthy tree with no flowers in spring
common_problems.solution: Withhold all irrigation from November through February. Lychee requires 100-200 hours below 60°F AND drought stress to trigger bloom. SW Florida provides both naturally in good years.

common_problems.symptoms: Ripe fruits splitting on the tree before harvest
common_problems.solution: Inconsistent irrigation during fruit development causes cracking. Maintain consistent moisture as fruits approach ripeness.

common_problems.symptoms: Velvety or furry patches on new leaves, distorted growth
common_problems.solution: Sulfur spray or abamectin. Erinose mite is a significant pest of lychee in Florida.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Air-layered trees available at tropical fruit nurseries. Fruitscapes and Possum Trot Nursery are good sources in SW Florida.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at tropical fruit nurseries — buy air-layered trees only
plants.expert_tips: SW Florida is one of the best places in the continental US to grow lychee — the climate provides exactly what the tree needs: warm wet summers for fruit development and cool dry winters for bloom initiation. The single most important practice is withholding all irrigation from November through February. Gardeners who water their lychee year-round rarely get fruit. Stop watering completely in November and don't restart until you see flower buds emerging — usually February.
plants.fun_fact: Lychee has been cultivated in China for over 2,000 years and was a tribute fruit to the imperial court — the Tang Dynasty Emperor Xuanzong famously had fresh lychees rushed to his favorite consort Yang Guifei via relay horse from the subtropical south to the northern capital, a journey of over 1,000 miles, just to satisfy her craving for the fruit. This story is commemorated in countless Chinese poems and historical accounts.
plants.traditional_uses: Cultivated in China for 2,000+ years. Fresh fruit eaten as a delicacy. Dried fruit used in Chinese traditional medicine as a tonic for the liver and kidneys. Not part of Florida indigenous traditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from China. No invasive concerns in Florida. SW Florida is near the northern limit of reliable lychee production in the US — the climate here is genuinely well-suited.

plants.expert_tips: Carambola is one of the most practical tropical fruit trees for SW Florida — it produces multiple crops per year, starts fruiting relatively quickly from grafted trees, and the fruit is excellent fresh with a sweet-tart flavor that varies by variety. Choose 'Arkin' for reliable sweet fruit. The star shape when sliced cross-sectionally makes it one of the most distinctive and attractive tropical fruits.
plants.fun_fact: The star shape of sliced carambola comes from its five prominent longitudinal ribs — the cross-section of each rib creates one point of the star. The fruit is so visually distinctive that 'starfruit' has become the primary common name in most English-speaking markets. The flavor ranges from extremely tart in some varieties (used for cooking) to very sweet in named dessert varieties like 'Arkin.'
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Southeast Asia. Cultivated throughout tropical Asia for centuries. Used in Chinese traditional medicine and Ayurvedic medicine for various conditions. plants.expert_tips: Sapodilla is the most underrated fruit tree in SW Florida — it tolerates coastal salt spray and drought that would kill most other fruit trees, produces beautiful glossy evergreen foliage year-round, and the ripe fruit has a flavor genuinely unlike anything else: a combination of brown sugar, pear, vanilla, and caramel that must be experienced to be understood. It is also the original source of chicle, the natural latex used to make chewing gum. Plant one near the coast where other fruit trees struggle.
plants.fun_fact: Sapodilla latex (chicle) was the original ingredient in chewing gum. The Aztec and Maya chewed chicle from sapodilla trees long before Europeans arrived in the Americas. When American entrepreneur Thomas Adams failed to find a commercial use for chicle he'd acquired from Mexico, he accidentally discovered its potential as a chewing gum base in 1869, leading to the modern chewing gum industry. For much of the 20th century, chicle was wild-harvested from sapodilla trees in Mexico and Central America.
plants.traditional_uses: The Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples cultivated sapodilla for over 2,000 years. The fruit was a staple food and the chicle was chewed medicinally. The wood is one of the hardest tropical woods available and was used extensively by the Maya for temple construction — sapodilla wood in Mayan temples has survived over 1,000 years.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Mexico and Central America. No invasive concerns. Exceptionally drought and salt tolerant — valuable for coastal landscapes where most fruit trees cannot survive.

plants.expert_tips: Common guava is one of the most productive fruit trees you can grow in SW Florida — it requires minimal care and produces abundantly. The caveat is the invasive concern: in south Florida's natural areas, guava seeds spread by birds and mammals and the tree establishes aggressively in disturbed habitats. Plant where you can manage fruit drop and keep fallen fruit collected, and don't plant near conservation areas. The fruit is exceptional — high vitamin C, distinctive tropical aroma, excellent for jams, jellies, and fresh eating.
plants.fun_fact: Guava has one of the highest vitamin C contents of any common fruit — a single guava contains 4-5 times the vitamin C of an orange. In South and Central America, guava juice and paste (guayaba) are consumed daily by hundreds of millions of people. The fruit is so important nutritionally in developing tropical countries that it has been called 'the poor man's apple.'
plants.traditional_uses: Cultivated throughout tropical America for thousands of years. The Aztec and other Mesoamerican peoples used guava fruit, bark, and leaves medicinally — leaf preparations for diarrhea (documented effective in modern research), bark preparations for wounds, and fruit as food. Introduced to Florida by Spanish settlers.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from tropical America. LISTED AS INVASIVE in south Florida — escapes into natural areas and wetlands where it displaces native vegetation. Plant only where fruit drop can be managed and away from natural habitats.

common_problems.solution: No cure. Greening is spread by the Asian citrus psyllid. Protect trees with systemic insecticides targeting the psyllid. Remove and destroy infected trees. Thermotherapy (heat treatment) is experimental. Buy certified disease-free nursery stock only.

common_problems.symptoms: Large mottled brown-white caterpillars eating leaves — resembling bird droppings to avoid predation
common_problems.solution: Handpick on small trees. The caterpillars become giant swallowtail butterflies — Florida's largest butterfly. Healthy trees tolerate feeding. Bt spray only if defoliation is severe.

common_problems.solution: Systemic insecticide (imidacloprid) soil drench or foliar spray. Critical to control as psyllid is the vector for greening disease.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. CRITICAL: buy only certified disease-free trees from licensed Florida nurseries.

plants.expert_tips: The spring citrus bloom fragrance is one of the most extraordinary sensory experiences in SW Florida — a single tree in full bloom can perfume an entire yard. Citrus greening (HLB) is the most serious threat to Florida's citrus industry and home gardeners — it is everywhere in Florida and there is no cure. The best defense is: (1) buy certified disease-free trees, (2) control Asian citrus psyllid with imidacloprid, (3) fertilize heavily to maintain tree vigor. Symptom management doesn't save an infected tree but can prolong production.
plants.fun_fact: Florida produces over 70% of the US orange juice supply. The giant swallowtail — Florida's largest butterfly with a 5-6 inch wingspan — evolved with the native hop tree (Ptelea trifoliata) but has completely adopted citrus as its primary host plant in Florida, becoming possibly the most common giant swallowtail habitat in the state. The caterpillar's bird-dropping disguise is one of the most effective camouflages in the butterfly world.
plants.traditional_uses: Citrus is native to Southeast Asia and Australia. Introduced to Florida by the Spanish — Ponce de León brought orange seeds to Florida in 1513, making Florida's citrus industry over 500 years old. Citrus has been central to Florida's agricultural and cultural identity ever since.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native. Citrus greening disease has devastated Florida's commercial citrus industry and is a growing threat to home gardeners. Giant swallowtail habitat value is a significant ecological contribution of citrus trees in SW Florida landscapes.

plants.expert_tips: Papaya is SW Florida's fastest edible return on investment — plant fresh seeds in spring and you can be harvesting fruit within 9-12 months. The main management considerations are drainage (papaya dies quickly in wet soil), sex identification (need females or bisexual variety for fruit), and hurricane vulnerability (the thick hollow stem topples easily in wind — stake young plants). Self-seeding papaya colonies that perpetually replace aging plants are a common and charming sight in SW Florida edible gardens.
plants.fun_fact: Papain, the enzyme in papaya that makes it an effective meat tenderizer, is so effective that papaya leaves were traditionally wrapped around tough meat cuts overnight in tropical cultures. Commercial meat tenderizer products often contain papain derived from papaya. The same enzyme is used in various pharmaceutical and industrial applications including contact lens cleaners and fabric processing.
plants.traditional_uses: Papaya originated in Mexico and Central America where it was cultivated by the Maya and other Mesoamerican peoples. Introduced to Florida by European settlers. The papain enzyme has been used medicinally throughout the tropics for wound treatment, digestive conditions, and as an anti-inflammatory. Leaves used as wraps for cooking throughout tropical cultures.

plants.description: Outstanding native understory shrub with glossy quilted leaves, small white flowers, and bright red berries eaten by many birds. Host plant for several hairstreak butterflies. One of the best shade-tolerant native shrubs.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Light irrigation in dry season — tolerates moderate drought in shade

plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy and rewarding, especially for shaded areas. One of the best native solutions for dry shade under large trees. Essentially no maintenance once established in appropriate conditions.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Critical component of native hammock understory. Berry crop feeds multiple bird species. Host plant for several butterfly species. Exceptional value for shade gardens.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe red berries. Remove pulp and sow fresh seeds immediately in moist well-drained mix. Seeds lose viability quickly — plant within days of collection.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings in summer. Take 4-6 inch cuttings, strip lower leaves, dip in rooting hormone, keep in humid conditions. Roots in 4-6 weeks.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow fresh seeds in moist mix, barely cover.
plants.germination_notes: Fresh seeds germinate reasonably well. Seeds lose viability quickly after harvest — plant immediately. Cuttings are more reliable.
plants.transplant_notes: One of the best shrubs for shaded spots in SW Florida — a genuine solution for the difficult dry shade under large oaks. Transplants easily from containers. Space 3-5 feet apart. Water weekly for first 3 months.
