plants.expert_tips: Seaside goldenrod is a myth-buster plant. Goldenrod is endlessly blamed for hay fever — a myth that has persisted for over a century. Hay fever is caused by ragweed (Ambrosia) which blooms at the same time and produces wind-borne pollen. Goldenrod pollen is too heavy to be wind-borne — it is insect-pollinated and does not cause hay fever. The vibrant fall bloom attracts an extraordinary diversity of butterflies, bees, and other insects. Plant it without any allergy concern.
plants.fun_fact: The hay fever myth about goldenrod was largely created by accident — ragweed and goldenrod bloom simultaneously, and the very visible goldenrod was blamed for the allergies caused by the inconspicuous ragweed blooming nearby. The myth was widely propagated and goldenrod was pulled from gardens for decades based on completely wrong information. Goldenrod is actually one of the most ecologically important fall wildflowers in North America.
plants.traditional_uses: Used extensively by indigenous peoples throughout eastern North America including the Seminole — leaf tea for fever and kidney complaints, chewed root for toothache, poultice preparations for wounds and skin conditions. One of the most-used medicinal plants in the eastern Native American pharmacopoeia.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to coastal habitats of Florida — one of the most salt-tolerant native wildflowers available. Critical component of coastal scrub and dune plant communities. Fall bloom provides essential late-season support for migrating monarchs.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for coastal and naturalistic landscapes. Clarify the hay fever myth in HOA presentations — goldenrod does not cause allergies.

plants.description: Native perennial with grass-like foliage and charming three-petaled purple-blue flowers. Bees and butterflies visit. Young leaves and flowers edible — used in salads. Naturalizes easily in garden beds.
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back after bloom season to encourage compact regrowth and secondary bloom.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy. Edible and ecologically valuable. Self-sustaining once established.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native spring wildflower. Bee nectar plant. Edible for humans. Self-sustaining.
plants.propagation_seed: Self-seeds reliably. Collect seed capsules when they begin to turn brown. Direct sow on moist soil.
plants.propagation_cutting: Stem cuttings root easily in water or moist soil.
plants.propagation_division: Easy — divide established clumps any time. Each division needs roots and stems.
plants.germination_method: Direct sow on moist soil surface.
plants.germination_notes: Self-seeds reliably. Division is the fastest propagation method.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun to partial shade. Moderate moisture. Adaptable to most soil types. Self-seeds and spreads to form colonies. Young leaves and flowers are edible — used in salads, with a mild slightly mucilaginous texture. Space 18-24 inches.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns
plants.looks_like_plants: Dayflower (Commelina diffusa) — both have similar blue three-petaled flowers
plants.looks_like_notes: Spiderwort flowers are symmetric with all three petals equal; dayflower has two larger upper petals and one smaller lower petal. Spiderwort leaves are long and grass-like; dayflower leaves are shorter and more oval.
plants.attracts_specific: Various native bee species, Bumblebee, Honeybee

seasonal_care.january: Cool dry season. Plants may be sparse or dormant. No irrigation needed.
seasonal_care.february: New growth emerging with warming temperatures.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous growth. Bloom beginning — charming purple-blue three-petaled flowers.
seasonal_care.april: Peak spring bloom. Bees active on the distinctive flowers.
seasonal_care.may: Continued bloom. Edible leaves and flowers at their best now.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season. Plants may go semi-dormant in heat. Allow self-seeding.
seasonal_care.july: Summer dormancy possible in peak heat.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Low spreading habit handles wind well.
seasonal_care.september: Regrowth from dormancy with cooler temperatures.
seasonal_care.october: Fall bloom possible. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.december: May go dormant. No irrigation needed.

common_problems.problem: No significant pest or disease problems
common_problems.symptoms: Very few pests or diseases affect this plant
common_problems.solution: One of the most trouble-free native wildflowers available.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales. Less common at big box stores. Very easy to propagate from cuttings or division.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales
plants.expert_tips: Spiderwort's combination of edibility, native status, and bee attraction makes it a unique value-add for the native garden. Young leaves are edible raw in salads or cooked like spinach, and the flowers are edible as a garnish. The three-petaled purple-blue flowers are distinctive and charming. It fills a useful role as a self-seeding low-maintenance native ground-level wildflower that provides bee food in spring.
plants.fun_fact: Spiderwort's common name is thought to come from the web-like silvery hairs that connect the flower petals when they are torn apart — resembling a spider's web. The genus Tradescantia is named for John Tradescant the Elder (c.1570-1638), one of the first professional gardeners in England and a plant collector who traveled extensively in Europe and North Africa.
plants.traditional_uses: Various Tradescantia species were important food plants for southeastern indigenous peoples — young shoots and leaves cooked as greens, roots used for food, and various medicinal preparations for skin conditions, heart ailments, and as an insect repellent. The Seminole and Calusa would have encountered this plant in wet edges and disturbed habitats.
plants.conservation_notes: Native throughout Florida in a variety of habitats. Common and secure. Provides early spring pollinator support and is an edible native wildflower with traditional food use.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for naturalistic plantings. Low-maintenance self-seeding native wildflower.

plants.description: Non-native host plant for monarchs and queens. Blooms year-round in FL. Best used alongside native milkweeds.
warnings: Non-native milkweed — blooms year-round which may discourage monarch migration south. Plant alongside native Asclepias tuberosa. Mildly toxic to pets in large quantities.
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back hard in October-November to simulate seasonal die-back and encourage monarch migration south. This is an important conservation practice.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy. Important monarch plant with caveats about year-round bloom and OE parasite. Best used alongside native milkweed.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Important monarch host plant with caveats. Best used with native Asclepias tuberosa. Year-round bloom supports pollinators but may interfere with migration.
plants.propagation_seed: Easy — collect dry seed pods. Surface sow on well-drained soil. Germinates readily.
plants.propagation_cutting: Tip cuttings root easily in 2-3 weeks. Wear gloves — milky sap is irritating.
plants.germination_notes: One of the easiest milkweeds to grow from seed. Self-sows in SW Florida.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Well-drained soil. Regular moisture. Grows fast and blooms quickly from seed. Plant alongside native Asclepias tuberosa for a complete monarch habitat planting. The combination of year-round (non-native) and seasonal (native) milkweed provides continuous support while maintaining natural migration cues.
do_not_plant_near: Areas where it cannot be cut back in fall for migration support
plants.looks_like_plants: Butterfly weed (Asclepias tuberosa) — native milkweed
plants.looks_like_notes: Scarlet milkweed has red petals with yellow-orange corona and smooth leaves with milky sap; butterfly weed has all-orange flowers and hairy leaves without milky sap. Both support monarchs. The milky sap distinguishes scarlet milkweed.
plants.attracts_specific: Monarch butterfly (primary host plant and nectar), Queen butterfly (host plant and nectar), Soldier butterfly (host plant), Bumblebee, Honeybee, Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Blooming year-round. No irrigation needed for established plants. Monarch caterpillars possible.
seasonal_care.february: Light cutback if leggy. Bloom resumes quickly.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous growth and bloom. Monarchs returning from Mexico migration.
seasonal_care.april: Heavy bloom. Critical spring nectar source for northbound monarchs. Do not spray.
seasonal_care.may: Heavy bloom and caterpillar activity. Water new plantings.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Continued bloom.
seasonal_care.july: Heavy summer bloom. Caterpillars present. No action needed.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Flexible stems handle wind well.
seasonal_care.september: Continued bloom. Important fall migration nectar plant.
seasonal_care.october: Critical fall migration month — monarchs moving south. Year-round bloom is why this plant concerns migration biologists.
seasonal_care.november: Bloom continues. Monarchs may linger on year-round blooming milkweed.
seasonal_care.december: Bloom continues year-round — the ecological concern is that year-round bloom may confuse migration timing.

common_problems.symptoms: Plant stripped bare by orange, black, and white caterpillars
common_problems.solution: This is the plant fulfilling its most important purpose. Do not spray. The plant recovers within weeks.

common_problems.problem: OE parasite concerns with year-round milkweed
common_problems.symptoms: Monarch butterflies appearing with deformed wings or dying
common_problems.solution: The Ophryocystis elektroscirrha (OE) parasite spreads more readily on year-round milkweed. If you observe unhealthy monarchs, cut all non-native milkweed back hard in fall to encourage migration and OE cycle disruption. Plant native Asclepias tuberosa as primary host.

common_problems.symptoms: Dense yellow aphids with black legs on new growth and buds
common_problems.solution: Strong water spray. Insecticidal soap — use carefully to protect butterfly eggs and small caterpillars.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers year-round. One of the most commonly sold butterfly garden plants.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Scarlet milkweed is the most widely planted monarch host plant in Florida — and there is a genuine ongoing debate among monarch scientists about the impact of year-round tropical milkweed on migration behavior. The concern: year-round bloom may discourage fall migration south. The current consensus recommendation is to plant it alongside native Asclepias tuberosa and cut non-native milkweed back hard in October-November to simulate the natural seasonal die-back that cues migration.
plants.fun_fact: The vivid red and orange-yellow colors of scarlet milkweed flowers are a classic example of aposematic (warning) coloration — the same color scheme that advertises toxicity in monarch butterflies. The plant and the butterfly evolved together over millions of years in tropical America, each reinforcing the visual warning system that protects both from predators.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally throughout Central and South America — root and leaf preparations used for worm infestations, fever, and as an emetic. The plant is native to tropical America and would have been known to indigenous peoples throughout its range.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from tropical America. In Florida, the year-round bloom may contribute to OE parasite spread in monarchs. Best used in combination with native milkweed and cut back in fall. Still one of the most important supplemental monarch plants available despite the caveats.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved. The monarch connection is a strong community selling point.

plants.description: Classic reliable annual that blooms year-round in SW Florida. Bees and butterflies visit actively. Strong fragrance deters many garden pests. Flowers edible as a garnish.
warnings: Can cause mild skin irritation and mild gastrointestinal upset in pets if ingested in quantity.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: 2-3 times per week in dry season

plants.pruning_notes: Deadhead spent blooms to extend flowering. Replace plants in summer when they decline.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in fall-spring season. Summer replacement required. Outstanding cool-season annual for SW Florida.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Moderate butterfly nectar. Natural pest deterrence in vegetable gardens. Limited ecological value. Excellent ornamental.
plants.propagation_seed: Direct sow 1/4 inch deep in well-drained soil. Very easy and fast. One of the easiest flowers to grow from seed.
plants.propagation_cutting: Tip cuttings root easily but seed propagation is more practical.
plants.germination_method: Sow 1/4 inch deep in well-drained soil.
plants.germination_notes: Among the fastest and most reliable flowers to germinate. Children's gardening favorite.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Well-drained soil. Water regularly in dry season. Avoid wetting foliage. Interplant with vegetables for natural pest deterrence — the root compounds deter nematodes and the scent deters many flying pests. Space 12-18 inches.
do_not_plant_near: Areas where summer replacements cannot be managed — plan for summer die-off
plants.looks_like_plants: Signet marigold (Tagetes tenuifolia) — same genus, smaller lacy flowers
plants.looks_like_notes: French marigold (T. patula) has dense pom-pom flowers in yellow, orange, and red; African marigold (T. erecta) has large globe flowers and is much taller; signet marigold (T. tenuifolia) has tiny single flowers and ferny foliage. All are good butterfly annuals.
plants.attracts_specific: Monarch butterfly (nectar), Gulf fritillary (nectar), Various skipper butterflies, Honeybee, Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Cool weather favorites — marigolds perform beautifully in SW Florida's mild winter. Water 2-3 times per week.
seasonal_care.february: Peak cool-season performance. Heavy bloom. Keep watered.
seasonal_care.march: Continued excellent bloom as temperatures rise.
seasonal_care.april: Still performing well. Begin replacing with summer-tolerant plants if desired.
seasonal_care.may: Heat and humidity beginning to stress. Replace with more heat-tolerant species.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — marigolds struggle in summer heat and humidity. Replace if declining.
seasonal_care.july: Full summer heat — marigolds typically fail in SW Florida's summer conditions.
seasonal_care.august: Most marigolds will not survive summer in SW Florida — replace with summer annuals.
seasonal_care.september: Good month to replant marigolds for fall-winter season.
seasonal_care.october: Peak fall performance begins. Monarch migration — marigolds are a good nectar source.
seasonal_care.november: Excellent fall-winter bloom. Very heavy flowering.
seasonal_care.december: Peak winter performance — one of the best cool-season color plants.

common_problems.symptoms: Plant wilting, yellowing, dying in June-August
common_problems.solution: SW Florida summers are too hot and humid for most marigolds. This is normal and expected. Replace with summer-tolerant annuals and replant marigolds in September.

common_problems.symptoms: Stippled bronzing of leaves, webbing
common_problems.solution: Hose off leaf undersides with water. Miticide if severe.

common_problems.symptoms: Gray fuzzy rot on flowers in humid weather
common_problems.solution: Improve air circulation. Avoid overhead watering. Remove affected flowers.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers September through May. Available as seed packets year-round.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Marigolds are a fall-through-spring annual in SW Florida — the opposite of their role in northern climates. They perform spectacularly in the mild cool months (October through May) and typically fail in the summer heat. Buy transplants in September for fall color and again in January for spring color. The pest deterrence properties are real — marigold roots produce alpha-terthienyl which kills nematodes, and the scent deters whitefly, aphids, and other pests in vegetable gardens.
plants.fun_fact: Marigolds have one of the longest recorded relationships with human cultivation of any flower — they have been grown for over 2,000 years across multiple cultures. In Mexican tradition they are the 'flower of the dead' (cempasúchil) used abundantly on Día de los Muertos altars to guide spirits home with their scent and color. The same species is sacred in Hindu traditions and used extensively in religious ceremonies throughout India.
plants.traditional_uses: Widely used throughout their native Mexico and Central America for ceremonial, culinary, and medicinal purposes. Petals used as food coloring in Mexico and Central America (and commercially for coloring chicken feed and egg yolks yellow). Used medicinally throughout the Americas for skin conditions, digestive complaints, and anti-parasitic properties.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native annual from Mexico. No invasive concerns. Moderate supplemental wildlife value and genuine garden utility for pest management.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Very popular HOA annual for fall-spring color. One of the most commonly used seasonal annuals in SW Florida community landscapes.

plants.description: One of the best drought-tolerant color plants for SW Florida's full sun areas. Brilliant flowers that close at night and open in sunshine. Very low maintenance — thrives in hot dry spots.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — can cause vomiting and diarrhea if ingested in quantity.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None to minimal — drought stress triggers best bloom

plants.pruning_notes: Minimal — pinch back if needed for tidiness. Self-seeds in warm conditions.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: One of the easiest annuals for SW Florida's most challenging hot dry spots. Virtually indestructible in the right location.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Moderate bee attraction. Fills color role in extreme heat conditions where ecological plants also struggle.
plants.propagation_seed: Direct sow on bare sandy soil. Do not bury — seeds need light and heat to germinate. Germinates in warm conditions very quickly.
plants.propagation_cutting: Stem cuttings root extremely easily in sandy soil or even in dry conditions.
plants.germination_method: Surface scatter on bare sandy soil in full sun.
plants.germination_notes: One of the easiest plants to germinate in summer heat. Self-seeds in SW Florida.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun essential — flowers close in shade and will not bloom well without direct sun. Sandy or gritty well-drained soil. Minimal water — excessive irrigation reduces blooming. Excellent for rock gardens, sandy banks, coastal areas, and hot dry spots where other plants fail.
do_not_plant_near: Wet areas — absolutely requires dry conditions
plants.looks_like_plants: Purslane (Portulaca oleracea) — common weed relative with smaller yellow flowers
plants.looks_like_notes: Moss rose (P. grandiflora) has much larger flowers in vivid colors; common purslane (P. oleracea) has tiny yellow flowers and is typically a lawn and garden weed. Moss rose leaves are more cylindrical and needle-like; purslane leaves are flat and paddle-shaped.
plants.attracts_specific: Various bee species, Honeybee, Bumblebee

seasonal_care.january: Cool weather slows performance slightly but portulaca continues blooming in SW Florida's mild winters. Reduce irrigation.
seasonal_care.february: Good performance in mild weather. Water 2-3 times per week.
seasonal_care.march: Excellent spring performance as heat increases.
seasonal_care.april: Peak performance with rising temperatures and sun intensity.
seasonal_care.may: Heavy bloom. Heat loving — actually does better as temperatures rise.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — portulaca handles SW Florida summers better than most annuals.
seasonal_care.july: Peak summer performance — thrives in conditions that kill most annuals.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Very low habit handles wind extremely well.
seasonal_care.september: Continued excellent performance. One of the few annuals that performs year-round.
seasonal_care.december: Possible slowing in coolest weather. Reduce irrigation.

common_problems.symptoms: Flowers closed despite no obvious stress
common_problems.solution: Normal behavior — portulaca flowers close in shade and on cloudy days. This is an adaptation — the flowers close to protect pollen in rain and open when pollinators are active.

common_problems.symptoms: Plant collapse in soggy conditions
common_problems.solution: Sandy well-drained soil is essential. Does not tolerate wet feet. The drier the better.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Very widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. One of the most heat-tolerant annuals available.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Portulaca is the heat-tolerant drought-tolerant color solution for SW Florida's most challenging sunny dry spots — hot pavement edges, rocky slopes, beach-adjacent areas, full-sun spots with poor sandy soil. Where other flowers would immediately fail, portulaca thrives. The flowers close at night and on cloudy days — this is normal and not a sign of stress. A fully open portulaca in full summer sun is one of the most brilliant color displays available.
plants.fun_fact: Portulaca grandiflora was one of the first ornamental plants to be successfully grown in space. In the 1990s, portulaca seeds were sent to the Russian Mir space station as part of plant growth experiments. The plant was chosen because of its succulent adaptations to extreme conditions and its ability to grow in minimal soil media.
plants.traditional_uses: Portulaca oleracea (common purslane, a close relative) is one of the most widely eaten wild vegetables globally, used in Mediterranean, Middle Eastern, and Asian cuisines. Portulaca grandiflora (moss rose) is primarily ornamental, but the family's reputation for edibility and medicinal use spans many cultures.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental from South America. No invasive concerns. Limited wildlife value but fills an important role as color in the most extreme sunny dry conditions where native plants may also struggle.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for dry sunny borders, parking islands, and rock garden areas. Very low maintenance.

plants.description: The best shade-tolerant annual for color in SW Florida. SunPatiens perform in full sun through shade. Butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds visit.
warnings: Traditional impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) are no longer recommended by UF/IFAS due to invasive risk. Use SunPatiens or New Guinea impatiens varieties only.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Daily to every other day — keep consistently moist

plants.pruning_notes: Cut back by half if getting leggy to encourage compact bushy regrowth. Very forgiving of pruning.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy for SunPatiens varieties. Regular moisture is the primary requirement. Excellent for shaded color beds.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good supplemental hummingbird and bee plant in shade. No ecological value. Best used alongside shade-adapted native plants.
plants.propagation_seed: SunPatiens are typically sterile hybrids — seed propagation not applicable for commercial varieties.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy — tip cuttings root in 10-14 days in moist mix. Division of large plants also works well.
plants.propagation_division: Large plants can be divided — each division needs roots and growing tips.
plants.germination_notes: Propagate by cuttings only for SunPatiens varieties.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun through full shade — the shade tolerance combined with sun tolerance is what makes SunPatiens unique. Regular moisture essential. Well-drained soil. Space 18-24 inches. Excellent in containers, hanging baskets, and shaded flower beds.
do_not_plant_near: Dry areas without irrigation — needs consistent moisture
plants.looks_like_plants: Regular impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) — similar flowers but very different disease resistance
plants.looks_like_notes: SunPatiens/New Guinea impatiens have larger flowers and thicker glossier leaves than regular impatiens. More importantly they are disease-resistant. If a plant is simply labeled 'impatiens' at a garden center, verify it is not Impatiens walleriana which is devastated by downy mildew in Florida.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers), Gulf fritillary (occasional nectar), Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Best season for SunPatiens in SW Florida — comfortable temperatures and lower humidity. Heavy bloom.
seasonal_care.march: Excellent bloom continues. Begin light fertilizing monthly.
seasonal_care.may: Heat increasing — SunPatiens handles it better than regular impatiens.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — reduce irrigation. SunPatiens generally handles SW Florida summers with good drainage.
seasonal_care.july: Performance varies — SunPatiens is more summer-tolerant than regular impatiens but may slow.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Replace if severely damaged.
seasonal_care.september: Good performance resuming as heat moderates.
seasonal_care.october: Excellent fall performance begins. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.december: Excellent winter performance. One of the best cool-season shade plants.

common_problems.symptoms: Rapid wilting and defoliation — plant collapses without warning
common_problems.solution: Do not use regular impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) in SW Florida — it is devastated by downy mildew. Use SunPatiens or New Guinea impatiens only.

common_problems.problem: Root rot in poorly drained soil
common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, wilting, stem rot
common_problems.solution: Excellent drainage required despite needing regular moisture. Raised beds or amended soil helps.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Very widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Available year-round. Always buy SunPatiens or New Guinea impatiens — not Impatiens walleriana.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: The important thing to know about impatiens in SW Florida is the species distinction. Regular impatiens (Impatiens walleriana) — the traditional bedding impatiens seen everywhere for decades — is now effectively unusable in Florida due to downy mildew that destroys it completely. SunPatiens (Impatiens ×hybrida) and New Guinea impatiens (Impatiens hawkeri) are resistant to this disease and are the correct replacements. Always verify you are buying the right type.
plants.fun_fact: SunPatiens is a patented interspecific hybrid developed by Japanese plant breeder Sakata Seeds Corporation, released in 2006 as a breakthrough that combined the shade tolerance of regular impatiens with sun tolerance and disease resistance. It was one of the most commercially successful new plant introductions of the 2000s and fundamentally changed the impatiens market worldwide.
plants.traditional_uses: Not native to Florida — New Guinea impatiens is native to Papua New Guinea. Traditional uses are limited in the horticultural literature. Not part of Florida indigenous traditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental hybrid. No invasive concerns. Good supplemental wildlife value for hummingbirds and butterflies in shaded situations where native alternatives are limited.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Very popular HOA annual for shaded areas. Year-round color in shade is difficult to achieve — SunPatiens fills this role reliably.

plants.description: Striking annual with dramatic plumed or crested flower heads. Butterflies and bees visit actively. Seeds eaten by birds. Leaves and flowers edible. Very heat and drought tolerant. Pet safe.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: 2-3 times per week in dry season

plants.pruning_notes: Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom. Allow some seed heads to stand for birds.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy. One of the best summer annuals for SW Florida's heat. Edible leaves add kitchen garden value.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Bird seed source. Butterfly nectar. Edible for humans. Good summer heat tolerance.
plants.propagation_seed: Direct sow 1/8 inch deep in well-drained soil. Very easy and fast in warm conditions. Self-sows in SW Florida.
plants.germination_method: Sow 1/8 inch deep in well-drained mix in warm conditions.
plants.germination_notes: Germinates rapidly in warm conditions. One of the easier annuals to grow from seed.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Well-drained soil. Regular moisture. Drought tolerant once established. Space 12-18 inches. Both plumed and crested forms are equally good for wildlife. Leaves and young shoots are edible — a common vegetable in West and Central Africa and Asia.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns
plants.looks_like_plants: No significant lookalikes — the plumed or crested flower forms are distinctive
plants.looks_like_notes: The dramatic plumed or crested flower heads are unlike any other common garden plant. Both forms are instantly recognizable.
plants.attracts_specific: American goldfinch (seeds), House finch (seeds), Monarch butterfly (nectar), Gulf fritillary, Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Cool season — celosia typically slows or dies in cool weather. Replace in late December-January if needed.
seasonal_care.february: Direct sow seeds for spring crop or transplant fresh starts.
seasonal_care.march: Excellent spring performance as heat increases. Fast growth.
seasonal_care.april: Heavy bloom. Bees active on plumed flowers. Birds beginning to feed on seed heads.
seasonal_care.may: Peak performance with full heat and humidity.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — excellent summer performer. Continue bloom.
seasonal_care.july: Peak summer performance. One of the most heat and humidity tolerant annuals available.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Flexible stems handle wind moderately.
seasonal_care.september: Excellent continued performance. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.october: Bloom continues. Birds feeding on seed heads heavily.
seasonal_care.november: Good fall performance. Direct sow for winter crop.
seasonal_care.december: May slow in cool weather. Replace if declining.

common_problems.problem: Damping off in cool wet conditions
common_problems.symptoms: Seedling collapse at soil level
common_problems.solution: Use well-drained soil. Avoid overwatering seedlings. Better air circulation.

common_problems.symptoms: Stippled bronzing of leaves
common_problems.solution: Hose off leaf undersides. Miticide if severe.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Widely available at SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Both plumed and crested forms commonly available. Very inexpensive from seed.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Celosia is underappreciated in SW Florida gardens — it is genuinely one of the most heat-tolerant and easy annuals available, it feeds birds with its abundant small seeds, it is edible (leaves used as a vegetable in West Africa), and the dramatic flower forms are architecturally interesting. The plumed form (Celosia argentea var. plumosa) looks like flames; the crested form (var. cristata) looks like a brain or rooster comb — both are striking in different ways.
plants.fun_fact: Celosia argentea leaves and shoots are one of the most widely consumed leafy vegetables in West and Central Africa, where the plant is called 'soko' in Nigeria and other local names across the continent. It is a highly nutritious green vegetable rich in protein, iron, and vitamins. The ornamental varieties grown in Florida are the same species as this important food plant — the leaves are edible.
plants.traditional_uses: Major edible vegetable crop throughout tropical Africa and Asia. Leaves cooked like spinach or used in soups and stews. Seeds and flowers used in traditional medicine for eye conditions, diarrhea, and skin complaints throughout Africa and Asia. Not part of Florida indigenous traditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native annual with no invasive concerns. Good supplemental bird seed source and butterfly nectar plant.

plants.description: Large showy daisy-like flowers in bold colors. Bees and butterflies visit. Blooms best in fall through spring in SW Florida — tends to slow in peak summer heat. Pet safe per ASPCA.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: 2-3 times per week — avoid wetting crown and foliage

plants.pruning_notes: Remove spent flower stalks at the base. Remove damaged leaves. Divide crowded clumps.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Moderate difficulty — crown rot is a real risk. The specific requirements (morning sun, crown above soil, excellent drainage) must be met for success.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Moderate bee and butterfly nectar. Primary value is ornamental. Good cool-season color for shaded areas.
plants.propagation_seed: Possible but slow and variable. Start 10-12 weeks before desired bloom.
plants.propagation_division: Divide established clumps in spring. Each division needs a crown.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow on moist well-drained mix. Seeds need light.
plants.germination_notes: Division of established plants is faster than seed propagation.
plants.transplant_notes: Partial shade — afternoon shade is important in SW Florida's intense sun. Morning sun only is ideal. Excellent drainage. Plant with crown slightly above soil level to prevent crown rot. Regular moisture. Space 18-24 inches. Replace annually or divide established clumps.
do_not_plant_near: Full afternoon sun — plant on east or north-facing exposure
Wet poorly drained areas
plants.looks_like_plants: Rudbeckia (black-eyed Susan), Osteospermum (African daisy)
plants.looks_like_notes: Gerbera has much larger flowers (4-5 inches across) than black-eyed Susan with a smaller brown or yellow center. Osteospermum has smaller flowers typically in white and purple combinations. Gerbera's large size and bold color range are distinctive.
plants.attracts_specific: Honeybee, Various native bees, Monarch butterfly (occasional nectar), Gulf fritillary

seasonal_care.january: Peak performance — cool-season favorite. Heavy bloom. Water 2-3 times per week.
seasonal_care.february: Continued excellent bloom. Best season for gerbera in SW Florida.
seasonal_care.april: Bloom transitioning — still good but starting to slow as heat increases.
seasonal_care.may: Bloom slowing significantly in heat. May replace with summer annuals.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — gerbera typically struggles in SW Florida's summer. Consider replacing.
seasonal_care.july: Summer heat usually ends gerbera performance. Replace if declined.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month. Replace damaged or declined plants.
seasonal_care.september: Good month to replant gerbera for fall-winter season.
seasonal_care.october: Fall performance beginning. Replant fresh plants.
seasonal_care.november: Excellent fall-winter bloom. One of the best cool-season flowers.

common_problems.symptoms: Plant collapsing at soil level, rotted crown
common_problems.solution: Plant crown slightly above soil level. Never bury the crown. Ensure excellent drainage. Most common cause of gerbera failure in SW Florida.

common_problems.symptoms: White squiggly trails through leaves
common_problems.solution: Remove and destroy heavily mined leaves. Systemic insecticide for severe infestations.

common_problems.symptoms: White coating on leaves
common_problems.solution: Improve air circulation. Sulfur spray. Morning sun with good air movement helps.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Widely available at SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers fall through spring. Very widely sold as cut flower plant.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers fall through spring
plants.expert_tips: Gerbera's success in SW Florida depends on three things: morning sun (not afternoon), excellent drainage, and planting with the crown above soil level. Get all three right and gerbera blooms magnificently through the fall-spring season. Get any one wrong and the plant rots. The afternoon shade requirement is the most commonly missed — SW Florida's afternoon summer sun is too intense for gerbera even in its cool season.
plants.fun_fact: Gerbera daisy was identified as a significant air-purifying plant in NASA's Clean Air Study (1989), which found it effective at removing benzene from indoor air. While the practical air purification value in real rooms (rather than sealed chambers) is modest, the study created enormous interest in gerbera as a houseplant and is still widely cited in plant marketing.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to South Africa — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Used in South African traditional medicine for fever and chest complaints. Primarily cultivated as an ornamental worldwide.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental. No invasive concerns. Moderate supplemental bee and butterfly value.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Popular HOA seasonal flower. Replace seasonally for best appearance.

plants.description: Excellent shade-tolerant annual with trumpet-shaped flowers. Hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies visit. One of the best choices for shaded flower beds where most annuals refuse to bloom.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: Daily to every other day — keep consistently moist

plants.pruning_notes: Pinch back tips to encourage compact bushy growth. Deadhead spent flowers.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in shade with consistent moisture. Best shade annual for hummingbird and butterfly support.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good supplemental hummingbird and bee plant in shade. No ecological value. Best used alongside shade-adapted native plants.
plants.propagation_seed: Easy — surface sow on moist seed-starting mix. Tiny seeds — handle carefully. Good germination.
plants.germination_method: Surface sow on moist seed-starting mix — do not bury tiny seeds.
plants.germination_notes: Fast and reliable in warm conditions. Seeds are tiny — do not bury.
plants.transplant_notes: Partial to full shade — does not perform well in full sun in SW Florida. Consistent moisture. Well-drained soil. Space 12-18 inches. Excellent in containers, window boxes, and shaded beds. The unusual two-tone flowers with an open throat are particularly good for hummingbirds.
do_not_plant_near: Full sun — will not perform
plants.looks_like_plants: Wishbone flower hybrids look similar to each other — Crown series, Kauai series, etc.
plants.looks_like_notes: Various torenia series are available with different flower sizes and colors. All are essentially the same plant in different color combinations.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers — open throat is accessible), Bumblebee, Various native bees, Gulf fritillary (occasional)

seasonal_care.january: Excellent cool-season performance. Heavy bloom in shade.
seasonal_care.february: Continued excellent bloom. Best cool-season shade annual.
seasonal_care.may: Summer heat beginning — torenia is more heat tolerant than many shade annuals.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — torenia handles SW Florida summers reasonably well in shade.
seasonal_care.july: Performance may slow in peak heat but maintains better than regular impatiens.
seasonal_care.september: Performance improving as heat moderates. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.december: Excellent winter performance. Best season for torenia.

common_problems.problem: Leaf spots and rot in poor drainage
common_problems.symptoms: Brown spots on leaves, stem rot at soil level
common_problems.solution: Well-drained soil and good air circulation. Avoid overwatering.

common_problems.symptoms: Clusters of small insects
common_problems.solution: Strong water spray. Insecticidal soap if persistent.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers fall through spring. May be harder to find in summer.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Torenia is the best solution for shaded flower beds when you need color and also want hummingbird and butterfly support. The open-throated flowers are excellent for pollinators, and the plant handles shade better than most alternatives. It is more summer-tolerant than regular impatiens in SW Florida. Pair with wild petunia (Ruellia caroliniensis) for a complete shade butterfly habitat planting.
plants.fun_fact: Torenia is sometimes called the 'wishbone flower' because the two forked stamens inside the flower resemble a wishbone. The wishbone structure is functional — when a bee enters the flower to collect nectar, the stamens are positioned to deposit pollen precisely on the bee's back, ensuring efficient cross-pollination.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to tropical Asia — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Used in traditional Vietnamese and Southeast Asian medicine for various conditions. Primarily cultivated as an ornamental.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental. No invasive concerns. Good supplemental wildlife value for hummingbirds and bees in shaded situations where native alternatives are limited.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: Good HOA annual for shaded areas. Colorful and consistent in shade situations.

plants.description: Iconic tropical flower with striking orange and blue blooms. Hummingbirds and bees visit. Blooms nearly year-round. Very drought tolerant once established.
warnings: Mildly toxic to pets — can cause vomiting and nausea if ingested. Seeds are more toxic than flowers.
plants.pruning_notes: Remove spent flower stalks at the base. Remove damaged leaves. Divide crowded clumps every 5-7 years.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in full sun with excellent drainage. Among the most drought tolerant ornamental perennials available.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good hummingbird plant. Very low water use. High ornamental value. No ecological concern.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seeds when pods ripen and split. Remove orange aril from seeds. Sow 1/2 inch deep in well-drained mix. Germination is slow — expect 3-12 months. First bloom takes 3-5 years from seed.
plants.propagation_division: Divide clumps in spring. Each division needs roots and at least one growing point. Plants take 1-2 years to re-establish and bloom.
plants.germination_method: Sow 1/2 inch deep in well-drained mix at warm temperatures.
plants.germination_notes: Division is much faster than seed propagation. Seed-grown plants take 3-5 years to first bloom.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun for maximum bloom. Well-drained soil. Drought tolerant once established. Plant with crown at soil level. Space 4-5 feet apart. Clumps expand slowly by producing new offsets.
do_not_plant_near: Shaded areas — will not bloom
Wet areas
plants.looks_like_plants: White bird of paradise (Strelitzia nicolai) — same genus, much larger tree form
plants.looks_like_notes: White bird of paradise (S. nicolai) grows 20-30 feet tall with much larger leaves and white and blue flowers; orange bird of paradise (S. reginae) stays at 3-5 feet with the iconic orange and blue flowers. The size difference is enormous.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (adapted to the South African sunbird-pollinated flowers), Bumblebee, Honeybee

seasonal_care.january: Blooming actively in dry season. No irrigation needed for established plants.
seasonal_care.february: Continued bloom. Good month for dividing overcrowded clumps.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Possible summer rest period.
seasonal_care.july: Less bloom in peak summer heat. No action needed.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — very wind resistant once established.
seasonal_care.september: Bloom resuming with slight temperature drop.
seasonal_care.december: Peak bloom season begins. One of the most spectacular cool-season bloomers.

common_problems.symptoms: Healthy plant that never flowers
common_problems.solution: Most common cause is insufficient sun. Bird of paradise needs full sun for reliable bloom. Also: clumps become too crowded — divide every 5-7 years. Fresh divisions take 1-2 years to re-bloom.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, crown rot
common_problems.solution: Excellent drainage essential. Does not tolerate wet feet.

common_problems.symptoms: Crusty white or brown bumps, sooty mold
common_problems.solution: Horticultural oil spray applied carefully to leaf base areas. Systemic insecticide for severe infestations.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. One of the most widely sold ornamental perennials. Many sizes available.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Bird of paradise is the queen of SW Florida drought-tolerant ornamental plants — nothing else produces such exotic architectural flowers with so little care. The key to reliable bloom is full sun, good drainage, and patience with divisions. If your plant is not blooming, move it to full sun. Once established in full sun with excellent drainage it blooms virtually year-round with minimal care. The flowers last 2-3 weeks as cut flowers — one of the best cut flowers available from the home garden.
plants.fun_fact: Bird of paradise is pollinated by sunbirds in its native South Africa — the sunbirds land on the blue petal 'tongue' which depresses to expose the pollen-bearing anthers, depositing pollen on the bird's feet. In Florida, ruby-throated hummingbirds have adapted to visit the flowers, though the pollination mechanism was evolved for a different type of bird.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to South Africa — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. The Xhosa people of South Africa used the plant as a symbol of freedom and use it in ceremonial contexts. It is the official flower of Los Angeles, California.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental from South Africa. No invasive concerns. Good supplemental hummingbird plant. Low water use is an important consideration in water-conscious landscapes.

plants.hoa_notes: Excellent HOA perennial — low maintenance, drought tolerant, near year-round bloom, architectural form.

plants.description: Spectacular foliage plant with enormous heart-shaped leaves in stunning combinations. No significant wildlife value but extraordinary visual impact in shaded areas.
warnings: Highly toxic to pets — all parts cause intense burning and swelling of the mouth, tongue, and throat. Can cause difficulty swallowing and breathing. Serious emergency if ingested.

plants.pruning_notes: Remove damaged or yellowing leaves. Allow dormancy naturally in fall.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy in shade with consistent moisture. Toxicity requires careful siting away from pets.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: No wildlife value. Spectacular ornamental value for shade. Toxicity is a significant concern for pets.

plants.propagation_division: Divide tubers when dormant in winter. Each division needs at least one growing eye.
plants.germination_method: Not applicable — propagate by tuber division.
plants.germination_notes: Plant tubers 1-2 inches deep in spring.

A single bite of a caladium leaf can cause severe swelling of the mouth and throat that may require veterinary emergency treatment.
do_not_plant_near: Pet areas — highly toxic to dogs and cats
Children's play areas

plants.looks_like_notes: Caladium has smaller more patterned leaves in heart to arrow shapes; elephant ear has larger more uniform green or dark purple leaves. Both are aroids with similar toxicity profiles. Caladium is grown primarily for the intricate leaf patterns.
plants.attracts_specific: No significant wildlife attraction — plants do not flower significantly in landscape use.

seasonal_care.february: Tubers dormant. No action needed. Good month to plant fresh tubers.
seasonal_care.march: New growth emerging from tubers as temperatures warm. Water consistently.
seasonal_care.april: Fast growth. Spectacular foliage developing. Water regularly.
seasonal_care.may: Full foliage display. One of the best shade plants in SW Florida summer.

seasonal_care.december: Dormant in zone 9b. In zones 10-11 may maintain some foliage.

common_problems.solution: Plant in well-drained soil. Do not plant in cold wet soil — wait until late spring when soil has warmed. Store tubers dry in winter.

common_problems.symptoms: Foliage dying back in fall

common_problems.problem: Leaf scorch in too much sun
common_problems.symptoms: Brown scorched leaf edges
common_problems.solution: Caladium needs shade. Move to a location with less than 3-4 hours of direct sun.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Extremely widely available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers spring through fall. Tubers available February through April. Lake Placid, FL is the commercial production center.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at all SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers spring-fall
plants.expert_tips: Caladium is the absolute best foliage plant for SW Florida's shaded areas — nothing else produces such spectacular leaf patterns and colors in shade. The toxicity is genuine and serious but manageable: keep it away from pets and children who might chew on leaves, and handle carefully. The heart-shaped leaves with their intricate patterns of white, pink, red, and green are genuinely breathtaking in a shaded garden setting. Plant in rich moist soil for the largest leaves.
plants.fun_fact: Caladium tubers are grown commercially in Lake Placid, Florida — a small town in Highlands County that produces over 95% of the world's caladium tubers. The Lake Placid area is considered the 'Caladium Capital of the World' and hosts an annual caladium festival each summer. So despite being a tropical ornamental from South America, caladium has become one of Florida's most distinctive commercial crops.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to tropical South America — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Used in various traditional medicine systems in South America for skin conditions, though the extreme toxicity limits practical medicinal use.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no invasive concerns. No ecological value to SW Florida wildlife. Best used as bold accent in shade alongside native shade-adapted plants.

plants.description: Many non-native salvia varieties perform beautifully alongside the native scarlet sage. Mexican sage, black and blue salvia, and guarani sage all attract hummingbirds and butterflies constantly.
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back hard after each bloom cycle for maximum bloom production. Essential practice for all salvia varieties.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy. Some of the most reliable non-native hummingbird plants available for SW Florida.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Excellent hummingbird and butterfly plants. Best used alongside native scarlet sage for complete multi-species habitat. No ecological risk.
plants.propagation_seed: Possible for some species. Results variable depending on species.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy — the standard method for all salvia varieties. Take 4-6 inch tip cuttings, strip lower leaves, plant in moist mix. Roots in 2-3 weeks.
plants.germination_method: Variable by species — follow seed packet instructions.
plants.germination_notes: Cuttings are the most reliable propagation method for consistent results.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Well-drained soil. Drought tolerant once established. Space 2-3 feet apart depending on variety. Cut back hard after each bloom cycle to maintain compact form and trigger new bloom flush.
do_not_plant_near: Wet or poorly drained areas
plants.looks_like_plants: Native scarlet sage (Salvia coccinea) — same genus
plants.looks_like_notes: Non-native salvia varieties differ in flower color and form from native scarlet sage. Black and blue salvia has deep blue-violet flowers; Mexican sage has velvety purple-and-white flower spikes. Native scarlet sage has red tubular flowers. All are excellent hummingbird plants.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary — especially attracted to blue-flowered varieties), Rufous hummingbird (winter), Monarch butterfly, Swallowtail butterflies, Cloudless sulfur, Gulf fritillary, Various bee species

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Most salvia varieties continue blooming. No irrigation needed for established plants.
seasonal_care.february: Good month for hard cutback to 12-18 inches to rejuvenate. Fast regrowth.
seasonal_care.march: New vigorous growth. Heavy bloom beginning. Hummingbirds and butterflies very active.
seasonal_care.april: Peak spring bloom. Extraordinary wildlife activity.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — stop irrigation. Bloom continues.
seasonal_care.july: Heavy summer bloom. Most non-native salvias perform well in SW Florida summers.
seasonal_care.august: Continued bloom. Hurricane month — flexible stems handle wind well.
seasonal_care.september: Continued heavy bloom. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.october: Bloom continues. Critical fall nectar. Good planting month.
seasonal_care.november: Best planting month. Year-round bloom continues.
seasonal_care.december: Bloom continues. Dry season — reduce irrigation.

common_problems.symptoms: Tall bare stems with flowers only at tips
common_problems.solution: Cut back hard after bloom cycles. Salvias bloom on new growth — regular cutbacks are essential for best performance.

common_problems.symptoms: Yellowing, decline, death
common_problems.solution: Excellent drainage required. Salvias do not tolerate wet feet.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers. Specific varieties like 'Black and Blue' may require specialty nurseries. Many labeled simply as 'salvia' or by series name.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: The non-native salvia family for SW Florida includes some of the absolute best hummingbird and butterfly plants available. Black and blue salvia (Salvia guaranitica 'Black and Blue') produces the most intense deep blue flowers of any plant available for SW Florida and hummingbirds find it irresistible. Mexican sage (Salvia leucantha) produces velvety purple-and-white spikes in fall that attract extraordinary butterfly diversity. Combine these with the native scarlet sage for a multi-season, multi-color hummingbird and butterfly garden.
plants.fun_fact: The genus Salvia is the largest in the mint family (Lamiaceae), with over 900 known species — making it one of the largest plant genera on earth. The word 'salvia' comes from the Latin salvere meaning 'to heal' — reflecting the extraordinary range of medicinal uses found across the genus. Common kitchen sage (Salvia officinalis) is just one of hundreds of medicinally used species.
plants.traditional_uses: Many Salvia species have extensive traditional use across cultures worldwide — culinary sages in European tradition, ceremonial white sage (S. apiana) in Native American practice, and numerous medicinally used species in African, Asian, and American indigenous traditions. Salvia divinorum is used ceremonially by Mazatec peoples of Mexico. The non-native ornamental varieties in this entry are primarily cultivated for garden use.
plants.conservation_notes: Various non-native species with no invasive concerns in Florida. Excellent supplemental hummingbird and butterfly habitat value. Best used alongside native salvia (Salvia coccinea) for a complete multi-species planting.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved. Year-round bloom and hummingbird habitat value make this a popular HOA landscape choice.

plants.description: Sprawling coastal native that roots at nodes and stabilizes sandy soil beautifully. Large pink-purple funnel flowers attract bees and butterflies. Handles salt spray, drought, and heat. Excellent for slopes, dunes, and canal banks.
plants.pruning_notes: Trim stems back from areas where coverage isn't desired. Easy to control.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Extremely easy on slopes, banks, and coastal areas. One of the best plants for rapid erosion control on sandy slopes.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native dune stabilizer. Butterfly nectar plant. Erosion control. Year-round bloom. Coastal habitat restoration value.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect seed pods when dry. Seeds germinate readily.
plants.propagation_cutting: Stem cuttings with nodes root extremely easily in moist soil. Plant stem sections on slopes and water for 2-3 weeks.
plants.germination_method: Direct sow 1/2 inch deep in sandy soil.
plants.germination_notes: One of the easiest groundcovers to establish from cuttings on slopes and banks.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Sandy, well-drained, or coastal soil. Extremely salt and drought tolerant. Plant on slopes, banks, dunes, and coastal embankments for erosion control. Excellent for canal banks where it roots into the soil and stabilizes the slope. Not suitable for areas with foot traffic — this is a sprawling vine-like groundcover.
do_not_plant_near: High foot traffic areas — sprawling stems are a trip hazard
plants.looks_like_plants: Moonflower vine (Ipomoea alba) — same genus, white flowers
plants.looks_like_notes: Beach morning glory has thick succulent-like leaves with a distinctive two-lobed shape; moonflower is a vigorous upward-twining vine with large white flowers. Both are in the morning glory family but very different in growth habit.
plants.attracts_specific: Cloudless sulfur butterfly (nectar), Gulf fritillary (nectar), Various bee species, Sphinx moths (nectar)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. Established plants need no water. May look sparse but roots persist.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month for slopes and dunes. Stems begin growing.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous growth. Large pink-purple flowers beginning.
seasonal_care.april: Heavy bloom. Bees and butterflies active. Fast stem spread.
seasonal_care.may: Rapid stem spread — can grow several feet per week in good conditions. Heavy bloom.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — explosive growth. Stop any supplemental irrigation.
seasonal_care.july: Fast summer spread. Heavy bloom. Roots at every node stabilizing soil.
seasonal_care.august: Hurricane month — extremely wind and salt resistant. Stabilizes dune soil in storms.
seasonal_care.september: Continued growth and bloom. Good planting month for slopes.
seasonal_care.december: May slow in cool dry weather. Established plants persist.

common_problems.symptoms: Stems sprawling into unwanted areas
common_problems.solution: Trim stems back from areas where coverage isn't desired. Very easy to control with a weed whip or pruners.

common_problems.symptoms: Blackened stems after cold snap
common_problems.solution: Normal — the root system survives and new growth emerges in spring.

plants.where_to_buy_notes: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales. Also easy to propagate from stem cuttings collected along established coastal plantings.
plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at native plant nurseries and FNPS sales
plants.expert_tips: Beach morning glory is the definitive dune and slope stabilizer for coastal SW Florida. Nothing else covers sandy slopes and canal banks as quickly, as cheaply, or as attractively. The large pink-purple funnel flowers are some of the most beautiful in the native coastal plant palette. Plant stem cuttings on a freshly graded slope, water for 3 weeks, and walk away — by the following season the slope will be completely covered and rooted.
plants.fun_fact: Beach morning glory (Ipomoea pes-caprae) is one of the most widespread plants in the world — it grows on tropical and subtropical beaches on every continent except Antarctica. Its seeds are spread by ocean currents, and the plant establishes on beaches wherever the seeds wash ashore. The species name pes-caprae means 'goat's foot' in Latin — a reference to the two-lobed leaf shape that resembles a goat's hoof print.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally throughout the tropical world — leaf preparations used for treating wounds and stings (including jellyfish stings), gastrointestinal complaints, and as a poultice for skin conditions. The Calusa and Seminole would have used this plant extensively in their coastal habitats. Documented use for jellyfish sting treatment continues in coastal folk medicine traditions worldwide.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to coastal dunes and beach habitats worldwide including SW Florida. Critical for dune stabilization and coastal erosion control. Planting on canal banks and coastal slopes directly contributes to erosion prevention.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for slopes, canal banks, and coastal embankments. Excellent erosion control solution for waterfront communities.

plants.description: Succulent native groundcover with small pink star flowers nearly year-round. Extremely salt tolerant. Edible leaves with a salty flavor used in salads and cooking. Excellent for coastal properties and canal edges.
plants.pruning_notes: Trim to contain if desired. Very easy to manage.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Extremely easy in coastal conditions. Edible, salt-tolerant, and ecologically valuable.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Edible native coastal plant. Erosion control in tidal areas. Bee forage. Critical component of coastal saltmarsh habitat.
plants.propagation_seed: Seeds viable and can be scattered on coastal sandy soil.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy — stem cuttings root wherever they contact moist soil. Plant stem sections in coastal soil and water briefly.
plants.germination_method: Scatter on moist coastal sandy soil.
plants.germination_notes: Stem cuttings are the fastest and most reliable propagation method.
plants.transplant_notes: Full sun. Sandy, saline, or coastal soil. Extraordinary salt tolerance — grows directly in tidal zones. Succulent leaves store water. Edible — harvest young leaves for salads or cooking (salty flavor, no special preparation needed). Excellent for canal edges, tidal areas, and coastal erosion control.
do_not_plant_near: Inland areas without salt exposure — performs best in coastal zones
plants.looks_like_plants: Tropical purslane (Portulaca oleracea) — similar succulent appearance
plants.looks_like_notes: Sea purslane has narrow elongated succulent leaves and small pink star flowers; common purslane has flat paddle-shaped leaves and tiny yellow flowers. Both are edible coastal/disturbed-area plants. Sea purslane grows in saltier, wetter coastal conditions.
plants.attracts_specific: Various bee species (flowers), Wading birds (seed heads in tidal areas)

seasonal_care.january: Dry season. No irrigation needed. Bloom continues year-round.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month for coastal areas. No action needed.

plants.expert_tips: Sea purslane is rare among SW Florida groundcovers because it is both ecologically valuable AND edible — the succulent leaves have a pleasant salty flavor and are used in coastal salads and as a garnish in seafood restaurants throughout the Caribbean. The plant is genuinely easy to eat and adds a distinctive flavor. It is one of the most salt-tolerant plants in SW Florida's native flora — growing where most plants simply cannot survive.
plants.fun_fact: Sea purslane has one of the widest natural distributions of any plant on earth — it grows in coastal zones on every continent except Antarctica, from the tropics through the subtropics. It has been used as a food plant by coastal indigenous peoples worldwide for thousands of years. The genus name Sesuvium may derive from an ancient regional name for the plant in northern Africa.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Seminole peoples harvested sea purslane as a food plant along coastal areas. Used as a fresh vegetable and cooked green throughout the Caribbean and tropical Americas. The high mineral content from saline soil makes it nutritionally rich.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to coastal tidal and saltmarsh habitats. Important component of coastal estuarine habitat. Provides erosion control in tidal and near-tidal areas where few other plants survive.

plants.expert_tips: Beach verbena is the most intensely violet-purple blooming native groundcover available for coastal SW Florida. The color is extraordinary — a vivid blue-purple that photographs spectacularly and provides outstanding contrast to the warm oranges and yellows of companion plants like beach sunflower and blanket flower. It blooms virtually year-round in coastal conditions.
plants.fun_fact: Glandularia maritima is endemic to the coastal areas of Florida and the Caribbean — found naturally only in that region. Its genus name Glandularia replaces the older Verbena in taxonomic treatments — molecular analysis showed that the New World verbenas were sufficiently distinct from the Old World Verbena to warrant separation. The coastal species are among the most salt-tolerant in the entire genus.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Florida and Caribbean coastal habitats. The Calusa and Tequesta peoples inhabited the coastal areas where beach verbena grows. Various verbena family plants have documented traditional use for fever, pain, and ceremonial purposes throughout the Americas.

plants.expert_tips: Golden creeper is one of the most unsung native groundcovers for coastal SW Florida. The low spreading mat with small glossy leaves and yellow fruits is genuinely attractive, and the plant's ability to handle direct salt spray and pure beach sand makes it invaluable for the most challenging coastal conditions where almost nothing else grows well. The yellow fruits give the plant its common name and attract birds year-round.
plants.fun_fact: Ernodea littoralis is the sole species in its genus — a monotypic genus native to the coastal areas of Florida and the Caribbean. The species name 'littoralis' means 'of the shore' in Latin — an apt description for a plant found almost exclusively in coastal salt-spray environments. Its isolation as the only species in its genus reflects millions of years of specialized adaptation to coastal habitats.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Tequesta peoples inhabited the coastal areas where golden creeper grows naturally. The small yellow fruits were likely eaten opportunistically. Specific documented uses are limited in published literature.

plants.expert_tips: Gopher apple earns its common name honestly — it is one of the most critical food plants for the Florida gopher tortoise, which depends on the small sweet fruits throughout its range. Planting gopher apple in sunny sandy areas of a landscape that hosts or borders gopher tortoise habitat is a meaningful conservation contribution. The fruits are also edible for humans — small, sweet, and pleasantly apple-flavored when fully ripe. The plant is essentially indestructible in full sun sandy conditions.
plants.fun_fact: Florida gopher tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) are a keystone species — their burrows provide shelter for over 350 other species including gopher frogs, eastern indigo snakes, Florida mice, and hundreds of invertebrate species. Gopher apple is a keystone food source for this keystone species, making it doubly important in the ecological food web of Florida's upland communities.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa, Seminole, and other Florida indigenous peoples ate gopher apple fruits as a fresh seasonal food. The sweet white pulp was consumed raw. The plant was a recognizable and reliable food source in the dry sandy scrub and flatwood habitats where these peoples lived.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to Florida's dry sandy scrub and flatwood habitats. Critical food plant for the Florida gopher tortoise (a protected species). Gopher apple supports gopher tortoise populations, which in turn support the 350+ species that depend on gopher tortoise burrows for shelter.

plants.expert_tips: Bloodberry is one of the most ornamentally attractive native groundcovers for shaded areas — the translucent bright red berries arranged in arching clusters are genuinely beautiful and persist for weeks attracting birds. It naturally partners with wild coffee (Psychotria nervosa) and coontie (Zamia integrifolia) for a complete native shade understory planting that covers all light levels and provides year-round fruit and butterfly host value.
plants.fun_fact: The common name 'bloodberry' comes from the deep red juice of the berries, which was used as a natural dye in its native tropical American range. The juice stains skin and fabric a persistent reddish-pink color and was used for face and body painting by various Caribbean indigenous groups. The genus name Rivina honors August Quirinus Rivinus, a 17th-century German botanist who was one of the first to propose a systematic classification of plants based on flower characteristics.
plants.traditional_uses: Used throughout the Caribbean and tropical Americas as a red-pink natural dye for fabric, skin, and basketry. The Calusa and Seminole would have encountered bloodberry in the hammock understory habitats they inhabited. Specific Florida documented uses are limited in published literature.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to hammock understory and shaded coastal habitats of south Florida. Important berry crop for shaded understory bird habitats. An excellent complement to wild coffee and coontie for complete native shade garden plantings.

plants.expert_tips: Mondo grass is the most popular non-native shade groundcover in SW Florida landscapes — and for good reason. It is genuinely neat, tidy, maintenance-free, and tolerates the dry shade under large trees that kills most other groundcovers. For purely functional shade coverage without ecological pretensions, it is an excellent choice. For ecological value, pair it with native shade plants (coontie, wild coffee, bloodberry) in the same bed.
plants.fun_fact: Mondo grass has been cultivated as a garden plant in Japan and China for over 1,000 years. The dwarf form ('Nana') was popularized in American landscape design in the mid-20th century and became one of the most widely planted groundcovers in the American Southeast. The blue-black fruits, while mildly toxic, were traditionally used in East Asian medicine as a lung tonic.
plants.traditional_uses: Used in traditional Chinese medicine (ophiopogon tuber — 'Mai Men Dong') as a lung tonic, heart tonic, and for treating cough, dry mouth, and fever. One of the most widely used medicinal herbs in traditional East Asian medicine.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Japan and China. No invasive concerns in Florida. Minimal wildlife value. Best used alongside native shade-adapted plants rather than as the only shade groundcover.

plants.fun_fact: Liriope's genus name references the naiad Liriope in Greek mythology, the mother of Narcissus (after whom the narcissus plant was named). plants.expert_tips: Wedelia is one of those plants that is genuinely attractive and useful in the landscape but has proven to be ecologically damaging in Florida. If you have it away from natural areas with no risk of spread to wetlands or canals, managing it carefully is reasonable. If you have it near any natural water body, canal, or natural habitat, replacing it with native beach sunflower or frogfruit is the responsible choice. Both replacements provide the same ground-covering function with similar yellow flowers and zero invasive risk.
plants.fun_fact: Wedelia's aggressive spread mechanism — rooting wherever stems touch moist soil — is the same mechanism that makes it useful as a groundcover but also makes it nearly impossible to eradicate once established in a natural area. A single storm can distribute stem fragments across a wide area through water movement, each fragment capable of establishing a new colony. This combination of vegetative spread, viable seed production, and tolerance of moist conditions makes it one of Florida's most ecologically damaging invasive groundcovers.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Mexico and Central America. Used in traditional medicine throughout its native range for anti-inflammatory purposes. Planted as an ornamental groundcover throughout the tropics.
plants.conservation_notes: Category 1 invasive on Florida's invasive plant list — confirmed to be altering native plant communities, disrupting natural processes, and spreading in natural areas. UF/IFAS Florida Friendly Landscaping program advises against planting. Consider replacing existing plantings near natural areas.

plants.expert_tips: Oyster plant is genuinely attractive — the purple and green sword-like leaves are bold and ornamental — but the combination of invasive listing, pet toxicity, and skin-irritating sap means it warrants careful siting. In contained beds away from natural areas and with pets unable to access it, the ornamental value is real. In landscapes near natural habitats or with pets, choose something else. Caladium provides similar bold foliage in shade without the invasive concern.
plants.fun_fact: Tradescantia spathacea causes a distinctive skin condition called 'garden rash' or 'contact dermatitis' in sensitive individuals. The sap contains compounds that cause redness and blistering with repeated exposure — many landscape maintenance workers develop sensitivity to it over time. Despite this, it is one of the most widely planted groundcovers in tropical and subtropical landscapes worldwide.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Mexico, Belize, and Guatemala. Used in traditional Mexican medicine as a poultice for skin conditions and wounds. The purple coloring of the leaves was sometimes used as a natural dye. Not part of Florida indigenous traditions.

plants.expert_tips: Longevity spinach is one of the most productive and low-maintenance edible plants for SW Florida's warm climate. The leaves are eaten raw in salads (mild flavor, slightly mucilaginous texture similar to malabar spinach) or lightly cooked. The plant is said to have anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties in traditional Asian medicine, and limited modern research supports some of these claims. For edible landscape purposes, it is one of the best shade-tolerant leafy greens available for SW Florida year-round production.
plants.fun_fact: Longevity spinach gets its common name from its extensive use in traditional Southeast Asian medicine as a longevity tonic — the leaves are believed to promote health and long life in Malay, Indonesian, and Thai traditional medicine systems. The plant is also called 'Sambung Nyawa' in Malay, meaning 'life connector' or 'life extender.' Limited pharmacological research has found anti-cancer, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant compounds in the leaves.
plants.traditional_uses: Widely used in traditional medicine throughout Southeast Asia — eaten as a daily health food and used medicinally for anti-inflammatory conditions, wound healing, and as a general tonic. Cultivated as a vegetable crop in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and China. Not part of Florida indigenous traditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Southeast Asia. No invasive concerns documented in Florida. Excellent edible landscape plant for partial shade situations.

plants.expert_tips: Okinawa spinach is one of the most beautiful edible plants available for shaded SW Florida gardens. The combination of ornamental purple and green leaves and genuinely edible, mild-flavored foliage makes it a unique dual-purpose plant. In a shaded bed alongside caladiums, it provides contrast and beauty while simultaneously producing edible leaves year-round. The raw leaves have a mild earthy flavor and slightly mucilaginous texture — excellent in salads with stronger-flavored dressings.
plants.fun_fact: Okinawa spinach is named for the Japanese island of Okinawa, where it has been a traditional staple vegetable for centuries. Okinawa is famous for having one of the world's highest concentrations of centenarians — people living to 100 or beyond. The Okinawan diet, which traditionally includes Gynura bicolor, has been studied extensively for its potential role in longevity. Whether the spinach contributes to that longevity is unknown, but the plant does contain significant antioxidant compounds including anthocyanins (responsible for the purple color).
plants.traditional_uses: Traditional vegetable of Okinawa, Japan, and throughout Southeast Asia. Eaten raw in salads, as a cooked green, and used medicinally for digestive conditions and as an anti-inflammatory food. Common in Chinese, Filipino, and Malaysian cuisine as a fresh or cooked vegetable.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Southeast Asia. No invasive concerns in Florida. Excellent dual-purpose edible and ornamental groundcover.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native year-round monarch, queen, and soldier butterfly host plant. Vine form fits spaces where milkweed cannot. Critical monarch conservation plant.

Unlike the non-native scarlet milkweed (Asclepias curassavica), this native vine does not grow as aggressively and has a more natural seasonal bloom cycle that better supports monarch migration. Plant alongside native Asclepias tuberosa for a complete native milkweed habitat.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns

plants.looks_like_notes: Twine vine is a vining plant with twining stems and white clustered flowers; scarlet milkweed is an upright bushy plant with red and yellow flowers. Both support monarchs. The vining habit of Funastrum clausum is diagnostic.
