plants.expert_tips: Twine vine is an underused native ecological gem — it's one of the only native vines in SW Florida that functions as a milkweed host plant for monarchs and queens, and it does so year-round without the OE parasite concerns associated with the non-native tropical milkweed. Because it's a vine rather than an upright plant it can be trained on fences, shrubs, and trellises in spaces where traditional milkweed wouldn't fit. It's the native milkweed option for gardens where space is limited.
plants.fun_fact: Funastrum clausum was previously classified in the genus Sarcostemma and is sometimes still found under that name in older field guides. The molecular phylogenetics that led to its reclassification also helped clarify its relationship to other milkweed family plants — despite looking very different from the typical milkweed (Asclepias), it shares the same chemical profile of cardiac glycosides that make monarch butterflies unpalatable to predators.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Florida, the Caribbean, and tropical America. The Calusa and Seminole inhabited coastal and hammock habitats where this vine grows. Specific documented traditional uses are limited in published literature.
plants.conservation_notes: Native perennial milkweed vine of Florida's coastal and disturbed habitats. One of the best year-round monarch host plants available with appropriate seasonal characteristics for migration support. Critical supplemental habitat plant for monarch conservation.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Native coastal vine. Year-round bloom. Bee and butterfly nectar. Salt tolerant. Well-behaved in the garden.

plants.expert_tips: Skyblue clustervine is one of the most underused native vines in SW Florida — it offers year-round blue flowers (one of the rarest colors in the native palette), extraordinary salt and drought tolerance, and completely non-aggressive behavior that makes it compatible with any garden size. The small individual flowers are delicate but the continuous clusters make an attractive year-round display. It is a genuinely rare combination of easy, beautiful, and ecologically valuable.
plants.fun_fact: The genus Jacquemontia is named for Victor Jacquemont, a 19th-century French botanist and naturalist who traveled extensively in India and died there of fever at age 31, having collected over 4,000 plant specimens in just a few years of fieldwork. The genus he was honored with contains over 100 species distributed throughout the tropical Americas and Africa.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Tequesta peoples inhabited the coastal areas where this native vine grows. The plant was part of the native coastal hammock and scrub plant community. Specific documented traditional uses are limited in published literature.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to coastal habitats of south Florida and the Caribbean. One of the few native vines that genuinely thrives in coastal salt-spray conditions. Excellent for coastal fence and trellis plantings.

warnings: Seeds and leaves are toxic to pets and humans — contain lysergic acid compounds. Keep away from children and pets.

plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy but vigorous. The night-blooming spectacular flowers are one of the most magical garden experiences in SW Florida.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Critical sphinx moth pollinator plant. Night fragrance experience. Native vine with unique ecological niche as night-blooming pollinator support.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect dry seeds — handle with gloves as seeds contain toxic compounds. Sow 1/4 inch deep in moist well-drained mix.
plants.propagation_cutting: Stem cuttings root readily in summer.

common_problems.solution: Moonflower grows very vigorously — prune regularly and direct growth onto the support. Plan for significant annual growth management.

plants.where_to_buy_local: Available at most SW Florida nurseries and big box garden centers
plants.expert_tips: Moonflower creates one of the most magical garden experiences in SW Florida — sitting outside at dusk and watching the enormous white flowers spiraling open in real time (the flowers open in a few minutes and the spiraling motion is visible) is genuinely spectacular. The fragrance, which carries strongly at night, is extraordinary. Plant near a patio or outdoor dining area where you will sit in the evening. Note the seed toxicity — remove seed pods in gardens with children.
plants.fun_fact: Moonflower flowers open in as little as 3-5 minutes at dusk, and the spiraling opening motion is fast enough to watch in real time. The flowers are pollinated by hawk moths (sphinx moths) that navigate by ultraviolet light — the white flowers reflect UV light brilliantly, making them visible to moths even before human eyes can see them well. The flowers close by mid-morning and are not recycled — each bloom lasts one night only.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to tropical America. Used medicinally by indigenous peoples throughout Central and South America — the seeds contain lysergic acid amide (LSA), a compound related to LSD, which was used in ceremonial and ritual contexts by various Mesoamerican cultures including the Aztec. The morning glory family was one of the most important plants in Mesoamerican ritual traditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to tropical America including Florida. No invasive concerns. The night-blooming flowers support sphinx moths that are important nighttime pollinators for many other plants.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for arbors and trellises. Night-blooming nature makes it a garden conversation piece.

plants.pruning_notes: Prune in late winter while dormant. Remove dead wood and train new growth to support. Annual pruning to fruiting spurs improves production.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy once established. Native vine adapted to SW Florida conditions. Annual pruning is the primary management requirement.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Edible fruit for humans and 10+ wildlife species. Native vine. Fall color. Host plant for moths. Maximum dual-use ecological and food value.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe grapes. Remove pulp, cold stratify 90 days, sow in moist mix.
plants.propagation_cutting: Hardwood cuttings in winter root reliably. Semi-hardwood cuttings in summer also work.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratify 90 days, sow in moist well-drained mix.
plants.germination_notes: Hardwood cuttings in late winter are the fastest and most reliable propagation method.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Sandy to loamy well-drained soil. Drought tolerant once established. Needs very sturdy support — a mature muscadine can be very heavy. Best on a sturdy fence, arbor, or strong trellis. Plant two or more vines for best fruit production — some varieties need cross-pollination. Named varieties produce larger, sweeter fruit than wild seedlings.
do_not_plant_near: Areas where very vigorous growth cannot be managed — this vine grows very large
plants.looks_like_plants: Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia) — both are native woody vines with similar habitat
plants.looks_like_notes: Muscadine has simple rounded leaves; Virginia creeper has distinctive 5-leaflet compound leaves. Both climb by tendrils but Virginia creeper uses adhesive pads while muscadine uses coiling tendrils that wrap around supports.
plants.attracts_specific: American robin (primary fruit consumer), Gray catbird, Cedar waxwing, Eastern bluebird, Northern mockingbird, Red-bellied woodpecker, Various thrush species, White-tailed deer, Raccoon, Gray squirrel, Sphinx moth caterpillars (host plant)

seasonal_care.february: Good planting month. Prune to shape before spring growth.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous spring growth — one of the fastest-emerging vines. Prune to desired size before growth gets ahead of you.

seasonal_care.may: Fast growth continuing. Pollination occurring. End of dry season.
seasonal_care.june: Rainy season — explosive growth. Green grape clusters developing.
seasonal_care.july: Grapes developing and ripening from green to purple-black. Wildlife feeding heavily.
seasonal_care.august: Grape harvest time — pick ripe clusters for jam, jelly, or eating fresh. Hurricane month.

seasonal_care.december: Dormant. Bare vine. Structural form visible.

common_problems.solution: Plant disease-resistant muscadine varieties. Remove and destroy infected vines. No cure.

common_problems.symptoms: Grapes disappearing before fully ripe
common_problems.solution: Partially accept as wildlife sharing — muscadine is a native wildlife plant. Use bird netting if you want to secure the harvest.

plants.expert_tips: Muscadine grapes are one of the most productive edible vines for SW Florida — they are specifically adapted to the southeastern US climate and disease pressures, unlike European wine grapes which struggle here. Named varieties like 'Ison,' 'Supreme,' and 'Cowart' produce large high-quality fruit. The grapes make exceptional jam, jelly, juice, and wine. Wildlife consumes them enthusiastically — raccoons, birds, and squirrels all find the fruit irresistible.
plants.fun_fact: Muscadine grapes contain extremely high levels of resveratrol and other antioxidants — significantly higher than European wine grapes. The thick skin and seeds (which are typically discarded in wine production but present in muscadine) contain particularly high concentrations. Research into muscadine's potential anti-cancer and cardiovascular benefits has been ongoing for decades at major universities in the southeastern US.
plants.traditional_uses: One of the most important native fruits for indigenous peoples of the southeastern US including the Seminole. Eaten fresh, dried into a raisin-like product, and used in various food preparations. The vine itself was used for basketry weaving. The leaves and stems were used medicinally for various conditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Native throughout the southeastern US including Florida. Important food source for wildlife throughout its range. The named varieties bred for fruit production are derived from wild Florida muscadine stock.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval varies — vigorous growth and fruit drop may concern some HOAs. Named as an edible landscape plant with wildlife habitat value for best HOA reception.

plants.description: Unusual native vine-like perennial with small lavender-pink daisy flowers that bloom in fall and winter — critically important late-season nectar when most other plants have finished.
plants.pruning_notes: Cut back hard to 6-12 inches in spring after bloom ends. Regrows vigorously for next fall bloom. Do not prune in fall — you will remove the flower buds.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy. Prune in spring, ignore all summer, enjoy the fall-winter bloom. Critical ecological timing makes it irreplaceable.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Critical fall-winter nectar for monarchs and fall pollinators. Bloom timing fills gap when almost no other plants provide nectar. Native vine-like scrambler.
plants.propagation_seed: Tiny seeds dispersed by wind. Scatter on moist soil in fall. Self-seeds in appropriate conditions.
plants.propagation_cutting: Stem cuttings in summer root in 2-3 weeks.
plants.germination_notes: Division of established plants is the fastest propagation method.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Moderate moisture. Well-drained soil. Scrambles over shrubs, fences, and hedges rather than twining like a typical vine. Prune back hard in spring to control size — it will regrow vigorously for a fall bloom. The fall-winter bloom timing is ecologically critical for monarchs, other migrating butterflies, and resident bees.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns
plants.looks_like_plants: Other aster family plants — Conoclinium, Liatris
plants.looks_like_notes: Climbing aster scrambles over other plants and has small lavender-pink daisy flowers with yellow centers; blue mistflower has blue-purple fluffy flowers with no ray petals; blazing star has tall purple spikes. All are ecologically valuable fall-blooming natives.
plants.attracts_specific: Monarch butterfly (critical fall migration nectar), Various swallowtail butterflies, American lady butterfly, Gulf fritillary, Bumblebee (critical late-season colony building), Honeybee, Native solitary bees

seasonal_care.november: Peak bloom — covered in small lavender-pink daisy flowers. Critical fall migration nectar.
seasonal_care.december: Heavy bloom continuing through early winter.

plants.expert_tips: Climbing aster is ecologically irreplaceable for fall-winter pollinator support in SW Florida — it blooms from October through February when almost nothing else is providing nectar, filling a critical gap for monarchs, other butterflies, and late-season bees. Plant it to scramble over an existing shrub or fence and simply cut it back to the ground in spring — it regrows fast and blooms reliably every fall. The timing cannot be replicated by other plants.
plants.fun_fact: Climbing aster was formerly classified in the genus Aster until DNA analysis revealed that the North American asters are not closely related to the European Aster species they resemble — they have evolved similar flower forms through convergent evolution. The North American asters were reclassified into the genus Symphyotrichum, a change that has been controversial among gardeners who prefer the traditional name.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Florida's wetland edges and disturbed habitats. The Seminole and other Florida peoples recognized this plant as part of the wetland edge plant community. Various Aster/Symphyotrichum species have been used medicinally by indigenous groups throughout North America for fever, pain, and respiratory conditions.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to the southeastern US including Florida. Critical fall-winter pollinator plant. The bloom timing fills an ecological gap that few other plants address.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval may require framing as a wildlife habitat plant with fall-winter bloom value. The scrambling habit may not suit formal landscapes — site on informal fences or naturalistic shrub borders.

plants.description: Native woody vine with stunning trumpet-shaped orange and red flowers in spring that hummingbirds love. Named for the cross pattern visible in the stem cross-section. Better behaved than trumpet vine.

water_needs_detail.established_frequency: None to occasional — rainfall sufficient once established

plants.pruning_notes: Prune after the spring bloom ends. Do not prune in late summer or fall — removes flower buds.
plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Easy once established. Outstanding hummingbird plant with well-behaved habit.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Outstanding hummingbird plant. Native vine with spectacular spring bloom. Better alternative to invasive trumpet vine.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect dry seed pods. Sow seeds in moist well-drained mix. Cold stratification improves germination.
plants.propagation_cutting: Semi-hardwood cuttings in summer root moderately well.
plants.germination_method: Cold stratify 30 days, sow in moist mix.
plants.germination_notes: Cuttings are faster than seed propagation.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Well-drained soil. Drought tolerant once established. Clings by branched tendrils with adhesive tips — attaches to wire, wood, and masonry without additional support (but less aggressively than Virginia creeper). Better-behaved than trumpet vine (Campsis radicans). Excellent on arbors, pergolas, and sturdy fences.
do_not_plant_near: Deep shade — needs some sun for bloom
plants.looks_like_plants: Trumpet vine (Campsis radicans) — similar orange-red trumpet flowers
plants.looks_like_notes: Crossvine has smaller more tubular flowers (bicolored orange-red with yellow throat) and pinnate leaves with 2 leaflets plus a branched tendril; trumpet vine has larger pure orange flowers and pinnate leaves with 7-11 leaflets. Crossvine is much better behaved — trumpet vine spreads aggressively by suckers.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (primary — shaped for hummingbird pollination), Rufous hummingbird (winter migrant), Various bee species, Hummingbird clearwing moth

seasonal_care.january: Evergreen in SW Florida. No irrigation needed. No bloom yet.
seasonal_care.february: Good planting month. No action needed.
seasonal_care.march: Vigorous spring growth. Orange-red flower buds forming.

common_problems.solution: At least 4-6 hours direct sun for reliable bloom. Partial shade is acceptable but full shade prevents blooming.

common_problems.symptoms: Brown scorched leaf edges
common_problems.solution: Afternoon shade is appreciated in SW Florida's intense heat. East-facing plantings perform well.

plants.expert_tips: Crossvine is one of the most rewarding native hummingbird vines for SW Florida — the spring bloom of orange and red trumpet flowers is spectacular and hummingbirds find it irresistible. Unlike the invasive-adjacent trumpet vine (Campsis radicans), crossvine is well-behaved and does not spread aggressively. The common name comes from the cross-shaped pith pattern visible in a stem cross-section — a genuinely interesting botanical detail to share with garden visitors.
plants.fun_fact: The crossvine gets its common name from the distinctive cross-shaped pith pattern visible when you cut the stem horizontally — four sections of pith in a cross or plus-sign arrangement. This feature is unique to Bignonia and is how the vine has been identified in traditional botanical literature for centuries. Cut a stem and show it to visitors — it's a reliable conversation piece.
plants.traditional_uses: Native throughout the southeastern US including Florida. Various southeastern indigenous peoples used the crushed vine medicinally as a poultice for swelling and pain. The strong flexible stems were used for cordage and binding. Specific Seminole uses are documented in ethnobotanical literature.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to the southeastern US. One of the best native hummingbird vines available for SW Florida. Well-behaved alternative to invasive-adjacent trumpet vine.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for arbors and sturdy fences. Spring hummingbird activity is a strong community asset.

warnings: Toxic to pets — all parts can cause vomiting and gastrointestinal distress if ingested.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good hummingbird and butterfly plant in shade. Distinctive flowers. Limited ecological value but fills real niche for shaded flowering vines.

Train on a shaded fence or trellis where few other flowering vines perform.

plants.looks_like_notes: The distinctive architecture — inflated white calyx with projecting bright red petals — is unlike any other common SW Florida vine.
plants.attracts_specific: Ruby-throated hummingbird (flowers), Gulf fritillary (nectar), Monarch butterfly (occasional nectar), Various bee species

plants.expert_tips: Bleeding heart vine solves the difficult problem of what to grow on a shaded fence or trellis that will actually bloom. Most flowering vines need full sun — bleeding heart vine flowers reliably in partial shade. The two-toned flowers are genuinely beautiful and unlike anything else in SW Florida's ornamental palette. The hummingbird and butterfly visits add wildlife value to what is primarily an ornamental selection.
plants.fun_fact: Bleeding heart vine is named for the famous bleeding heart flower (Lamprocapnos spectabilis) of temperate gardens, which it superficially resembles — both have a distinctive heart-shaped outer structure (the white calyx in Clerodendrum, the pink or white petals in Lamprocapnos) with a contrasting inner element. The plants are completely unrelated botanically — this is another case of convergent evolution producing similar flower architecture.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to tropical West Africa — not part of Florida indigenous traditions. Used in West African traditional medicine for fever and anti-inflammatory purposes.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native ornamental with no invasive concerns in Florida. Good supplemental wildlife value for hummingbirds and butterflies in shaded situations.

plants.hoa_notes: HOA approved for shaded fences and trellises. Distinctive bloom is a strong ornamental asset.

warnings: Can become invasive — monitor and prevent from escaping into natural areas. Remove seed pods before they mature near conservation areas.
plants.pruning_notes: Prune aggressively and frequently. Remove ALL seed pods before maturity near natural areas. This vine requires significant ongoing management.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Good hummingbird and bee plant. High ornamental value. Invasive seed spread potential requires diligent management.

Thunbergia grandiflora has large sky-blue to lavender trumpet flowers with no dark center. Always verify species before purchase. The invasive species is widely sold and must not be planted in Florida.

plants.expert_tips: Thunbergia is one of the most spectacular flowering vines available for SW Florida — the large sky-blue to lavender trumpet flowers are genuinely extraordinary in color and size. The management commitment is also significant: this is a very vigorous vine that requires aggressive pruning and diligent removal of seed pods to prevent naturalization. Plant only if you can commit to that management. In return it provides year-round color that is nearly unmatched in the vine category.
plants.fun_fact: The common name 'Bengal clock vine' refers to its native origin in Bangladesh and India (Bengal) and the way the vine's large leaves track the sun through the day with a slight daily movement. The clock-like regularity of this leaf movement was noted by early European botanists who named it accordingly. Despite the clock vine name, there is no scientific consensus that Thunbergia grandiflora is more sun-tracking than other large-leafed vines.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to Bangladesh, India, and southern China. Used in traditional Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine for skin conditions, inflammation, and respiratory complaints. Cultivated as an ornamental throughout the tropics for centuries.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from South Asia. Potential invasive concern in Florida — FLEPPC monitoring list. Remove all seed pods before maturity near conservation areas. Thunbergia alata (black-eyed Susan vine, a different species) is invasive in Florida — verify correct species when purchasing.

plants.description: Vigorous climbing vine with edible glossy leaves. Tolerates SW Florida's summer heat where cool-season spinach fails. Birds eat the small dark fruits. Productive dual-purpose food and ornamental vine.

plants.easy_to_grow_notes: Very easy in warm weather. The summer leafy green gap-filler that SW Florida edible gardens need.
plants.beneficial_score_notes: Edible summer leafy green production. Bird berry source. Fills critical warm-season leafy green production gap.
plants.propagation_seed: Collect ripe dark berries. Remove pulp and sow fresh in moist soil. Germination reliable.
plants.propagation_cutting: Very easy — stem cuttings root in 7-10 days in moist soil. The fastest propagation method.
plants.germination_method: Sow cleaned seeds 1/2 inch deep in moist soil.
plants.germination_notes: Cuttings are faster than seed propagation.
plants.transplant_notes: Full to partial sun. Well-drained soil. Regular moisture for best production. Needs a support to climb — fence, trellis, or cage. Harvest young leaves and stem tips raw in salads (mild flavor, slightly mucilaginous texture like regular spinach when cooked) or cook like spinach. The red-stemmed variety (Basella rubra) is identical in use with attractive dark red stems and veins.
do_not_plant_near: No significant concerns

plants.looks_like_notes: The thick, glossy, succulent-textured leaves are distinctive. No other common climbing edible vine has similar leaf texture.

plants.expert_tips: Malabar spinach is one of the most practical edible vines for SW Florida because it solves the problem that conventional spinach has — conventional spinach bolts immediately in the heat and is essentially unusable in a SW Florida summer. Malabar spinach produces continuously through the hottest months when most leafy greens fail completely. The leaves are used exactly like regular spinach but with a slightly more mucilaginous texture when cooked.
plants.fun_fact: Malabar spinach is not botanically related to true spinach (Spinacia oleracea) — it's in an entirely different family. The 'spinach' name comes from the similar culinary use of the leaves as a cooked green. 'Malabar' refers to the Malabar Coast of southwestern India, part of the plant's native range. Despite the lack of botanical relationship, Malabar spinach has an excellent nutritional profile — high in vitamins A and C, calcium, iron, and antioxidants.
plants.traditional_uses: Cultivated as a food plant throughout tropical Asia and Africa for centuries. Widely used in Indian, Chinese, and Southeast Asian cuisines as a cooked leafy green. In Ayurvedic medicine, used for digestive conditions and as a cooling food. The purple juice of the berries was used as a food coloring and natural ink in China.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native from Asia. No invasive concerns in Florida. The birds that eat the dark berries in fall may spread seeds but the plant has not naturalized invasively.
plants.review_notes: Awaiting detailed research — fields marked unknown need verification
plants.hoa_notes: HOA approval varies — edible vine may require framing as an ornamental. Glossy leaves and cascading growth are attractive on a trellis.

plants.beneficial_score_notes: Edible tubers and leaves. Sphinx moth host plant. Ornamental foliage. Good dual-use garden plant.

Both edible and ornamental varieties are available — ornamental varieties have colored foliage (purple, chartreuse, bronze) but smaller tubers; edible varieties have standard green leaves and large tubers. Both are host plants for sphinx moths.

plants.looks_like_notes: Sweet potato vine has heart-shaped lobed leaves and produces tuberous roots; morning glory has more deeply lobed leaves and no tuberous roots. Both have large morning glory-type flowers when they bloom.
plants.attracts_specific: Sweetpotato sphinx moth (Agrius cingulata — primary caterpillar host), Whitelined sphinx moth (caterpillar host), Bumblebee (flowers), Various bee species

plants.expert_tips: Sweet potato vine serves double duty exceptionally well in SW Florida — the edible varieties produce food underground while functioning as a sprawling ornamental groundcover or climbing vine above ground. The ornamental varieties (blackie, marguerite, etc.) are some of the most striking foliage plants available for containers and beds. Both types host sphinx moth caterpillars — large green caterpillars with a distinctive rear spine that become beautiful hawk moths.
plants.fun_fact: Sweet potato (Ipomoea batatas) is one of the oldest cultivated crops in the Americas, with archaeological evidence of cultivation in Peru dating back 8,000 years. It is not closely related to the potato (Solanum tuberosum) despite the similar common name — sweet potato is in the morning glory family while potato is in the nightshade family. The confusion is so longstanding that it is now essentially impossible to disentangle in casual usage.
plants.traditional_uses: One of the most important food crops in both the Americas and Africa. Native to tropical America — cultivated by the Taino, Aztec, and other indigenous peoples for thousands of years. The Spanish brought it to Europe and Africa in the 16th century where it became a staple crop in many regions. The Seminole and other Florida peoples cultivated it in garden plots.
plants.conservation_notes: Non-native cultivated crop from tropical America. The sweet potato vine is an important host plant for several sphinx moth species whose adult forms are significant nighttime pollinators.

plants.expert_tips: Carolina jessamine is one of the most rewarding native vines in SW Florida — the late winter fragrance of the yellow flowers is extraordinary and it blooms before almost anything else in the native garden, providing critical nectar when the garden has been quiet for months. The toxicity is severe and real — this vine has killed grazing livestock and children who sucked the nectar from the flowers. Site it on a fence or trellis that pets and young children cannot access. In appropriate locations it is a genuinely exceptional plant.
plants.fun_fact: The flowers of Carolina jessamine are visually identical in color and shape to true jasmine flowers, leading to the similar common name — but the plants are completely unrelated and Carolina jessamine's toxicity makes it dangerous to confuse with edible jasmine relatives. The genus name Gelsemium derives from the Italian word for jasmine (gelsomino), reflecting the early confusion between these similar-looking but botanically and toxicologically very different plants.
plants.traditional_uses: Native to the southeastern US including Florida. Used medicinally by southeastern indigenous peoples in extremely small doses — Cherokee used root preparations as a sedative and for fever reduction, and as a treatment for facial neuralgia. The therapeutic dose is dangerously close to the toxic dose, making traditional use highly skilled and dangerous. The toxicity was widely documented and respected.
plants.conservation_notes: Native throughout the southeastern US. The winter-spring bloom is an important early-season nectar source for bees and hummingbirds. The severe toxicity requires careful siting but does not diminish the ecological and ornamental value when properly placed.

plants.expert_tips: Spikerush is foundational for canal bank and pond edge habitat in SW Florida. It grows where few other plants can (very shallow water, wet sandy substrate) and provides the low-level structure that fish spawn in and ducks feed from. Plant it at the water's edge in front of taller emergents like alligator flag and sagittaria for a complete native aquatic planting.
plants.fun_fact: Chinese water chestnuts — a common ingredient in Asian cooking sold in cans at every grocery store — are the tubers of Eleocharis dulcis, a tropical spikerush species related to the SW Florida natives. The crunchy white discs in stir-fries and spring rolls are the underground tubers of a plant nearly identical to the native SW Florida spikerush. Florida's native Eleocharis species produce similar but smaller tubers that are eaten by wildlife.
plants.traditional_uses: Calusa and Seminole peoples used spikerush as part of their wetland habitat management. The dense mats provided fishing grounds and the tubers were eaten by both humans and the wildlife they hunted.

plants.expert_tips: Maidencane is the dominant emergent grass of SW Florida's freshwater canals and ponds — if you look at any undisturbed natural canal bank you will see maidencane. It is the ecological foundation of the emergent plant community. Planting it along bare or disturbed canal banks establishes the framework that allows other aquatic species to colonize and creates productive fish spawning and waterfowl nesting habitat.
plants.fun_fact: Maidencane is so dominant in Florida's freshwater wetlands that it is used as an indicator species for ecological condition — the presence of healthy dense maidencane colonies indicates a relatively undisturbed freshwater wetland. The degradation of maidencane stands, often replaced by invasive cattail (Typha) or torpedo grass (Panicum repens), is a key sign of wetland disturbance.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa and Seminole used maidencane extensively in their wetland-adapted culture — the strong stems were used for basketry and mat weaving, the seeds were harvested as a minor food grain, and the dense stands provided cover for hunting and fishing.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to freshwater wetlands throughout the southeastern US including all of Florida. Dominant emergent grass of SW Florida's freshwater canal and pond ecosystems. Critical for canal bank stabilization and fish spawning habitat.

The cup-shaped yellow flowers that stand above the water surface are visually distinct from the flat white water lily flowers. The seeds are very popular with ducks.
plants.fun_fact: The seeds of Nuphar (pond lily) are among the most important foods for waterfowl in North American freshwater wetlands. Ducks dive for the seeds which fall to the bottom after the seed pods open. The Seminole and other Florida indigenous peoples also harvested the seeds as a food grain — they were dried and ground into flour or parched and eaten like popcorn.

plants.expert_tips: American lotus is one of the most dramatic and beautiful native plants in SW Florida's aquatic plant palette — the enormous pale yellow flowers 10+ inches across held on tall stems above the blue-green parasol leaves are genuinely spectacular. The architectural seed heads that follow the bloom are equally beautiful and widely used in dried arrangements. Ducks eat the seeds extensively in fall. Plant only in large ponds where the aggressive spread is acceptable.
plants.fun_fact: Lotus seeds have the longest documented seed viability of any plant — seeds of a related Asian lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) excavated from a dried lake bed in China germinated successfully after 1,300 years of dormancy. One American lotus seed was germinated after 237 years of documented storage. The extreme longevity of lotus seeds is due to a unique protective seed coat that prevents water entry while maintaining metabolic activity at extremely low levels.
plants.traditional_uses: American lotus was one of the most important food plants for indigenous peoples throughout eastern North America — tubers eaten like potatoes, seeds eaten fresh and parched, young leaves eaten as greens, and flower petals eaten. The Seminole harvested lotus from Florida's freshwater marshes. Every edible part was used extensively.

plants.expert_tips: Coontail is the most practical submerged aquatic for improving water quality in SW Florida ponds and canals. It absorbs the nitrogen and phosphorus that would otherwise feed algae blooms, provides critical fish spawning cover, and requires zero planting effort — just place stems in the water. If you have a pond with chronic algae problems, add coontail and you will typically see algae reduction within weeks as the plant outcompetes algae for nutrients.
plants.fun_fact: Coontail is rootless — unlike essentially all other plants, it has no roots at all, not even vestigial ones. It absorbs all water and nutrients directly through its stems and leaves. The feathery whorled leaves that give it the 'coontail' or 'hornwort' appearance are extremely efficient at absorbing dissolved nutrients. This rootlessness makes it the only plant that can be introduced to a pond simply by throwing stems into the water.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa and Seminole fished the freshwater lakes, ponds, and canals where coontail grows. The dense underwater masses are critical fish habitat — where coontail grows, fish congregate. The indigenous peoples understood this connection and used coontail-rich areas as prime fishing locations.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to fresh water worldwide including Florida. One of the most ecologically important submerged aquatics for freshwater ecosystem function — water filtration, fish habitat, and waterfowl food. Declining in many Florida water bodies due to nutrient pollution and reduced water clarity.

plants.expert_tips: Eel grass / tape grass is essential for establishing healthy freshwater and slightly brackish aquatic ecosystems. It is the primary food plant of Florida's manatees in freshwater canals and rivers. If you have canal access and want to support manatees, establishing native tape grass is one of the most direct contributions you can make. It also provides critical fish spawning habitat.
plants.fun_fact: Florida manatees (Trichechus manatus latirostris) are completely dependent on submerged aquatic vegetation like Vallisneria for their food supply. A single manatee eats 10-15% of its body weight in aquatic vegetation daily — over 100 pounds for a large adult. The loss of native submerged aquatics due to water quality degradation is one of the primary drivers of manatee population stress in Florida.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa and Seminole fished the clear spring-fed rivers and freshwater systems where tape grass was abundant. The dense underwater meadows were recognized as prime fishing habitat and hunting grounds for aquatic animals that fed on the grass.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to fresh and slightly brackish water throughout eastern North America including Florida. Critical food plant for threatened Florida manatees. Loss of tape grass beds throughout Florida's waterways is a significant conservation concern. Planting in SW Florida canals directly supports manatee habitat.

plants.expert_tips: Asian lotus is culturally and culinarily significant in SW Florida's large Asian community — the lotus root (available fresh in Asian grocery stores) is the rhizome of this plant, and the seeds are the lotus seeds used in traditional Chinese desserts. Growing your own provides access to fresh lotus root, which is genuinely superior to the canned product. The flowers are extraordinarily beautiful and fragrant.
plants.fun_fact: The sacred lotus has the remarkable ability to regulate its own temperature — the flowers maintain a temperature of 30-35°C (86-95°F) even when ambient temperatures drop near freezing. This thermogenesis is thought to attract cold-blooded pollinators (beetles and bees) in cool conditions. The lotus is one of only a handful of plants known to be thermoregulatory.
plants.traditional_uses: Sacred in both Hinduism and Buddhism — the lotus flower symbolizes spiritual awakening, purity, and divine beauty in both traditions. Cultivated in Asia for over 3,000 years as both a sacred plant and food crop. Every part is eaten: rhizome (lotus root), seeds, young leaves, and flower petals. The Calusa and Seminole would have had no contact with Asian lotus which was introduced by Asian immigrants.

plants.expert_tips: Taro is one of the most productive starchy food plants for SW Florida's wet shaded areas — conditions where most food plants fail. The corms (the edible starchy underground portions) must be thoroughly cooked (boiling or roasting) to destroy the calcium oxalate crystals — raw taro causes serious mouth and throat injury. But cooked taro is mild, starchy, and used extensively in Polynesian, Asian, and Caribbean cuisines. Poi, the traditional Hawaiian food, is made from cooked and pounded taro.
plants.fun_fact: Taro has been cultivated for so long — over 7,000 years — that no wild ancestor has been definitively identified. It is one of the oldest cultivated food plants on earth and was the dietary staple that enabled Polynesian colonization of the Pacific — essentially every Pacific island people brought taro as a fundamental food crop during their voyages. The calcium oxalate toxicity of raw taro is so well known that many languages have specific words for the burning sensation caused by eating it raw.
plants.traditional_uses: One of the most ancient and widely cultivated food crops globally — cultivated for 7,000+ years across Asia, Africa, and the Pacific. Every part of the cooked plant is eaten in dozens of cultural traditions. Florida's Seminole and other indigenous peoples may have adopted taro after European contact brought it from Caribbean trade routes.

plants.expert_tips: Cardinal flower is the single most powerful hummingbird attractor available for SW Florida wet gardens. The brilliant red flower spikes in July-October are shaped perfectly for ruby-throated hummingbird pollination and hummingbirds visit them essentially continuously throughout the bloom period. If you have a canal bank, pond edge, or rain garden, cardinal flower planted there will have hummingbirds visiting from the first flowers in July through frost. No other plant delivers this intensity of hummingbird activity in wet conditions.
plants.fun_fact: Cardinal flower is one of the primary plants that drove the co-evolution of ruby-throated hummingbirds in eastern North America. The flower tube length, angle, and red color are so precisely matched to the hummingbird's bill, head, and visual system that many botanists consider the relationship to be a near-exclusive co-evolved pollination mutualism. When hummingbirds decline in an area, cardinal flower reproduction suffers — when cardinal flower declines, hummingbirds lose a critical food source.
plants.traditional_uses: Used medicinally by many indigenous peoples throughout eastern North America — various preparations for respiratory conditions, fever, and headache. The Seminole and other Florida peoples recognized it as a wetland species. Used by some groups ceremonially. The toxicity was well known and medicinal use was carefully managed.
plants.conservation_notes: Native to fresh wetland habitats throughout eastern North America including Florida. One of the most important hummingbird plants in the eastern US. Increasingly scarce in the wild due to wetland loss. Planting at canal banks and pond edges contributes to habitat restoration.

plants.expert_tips: Golden canna is the native version of the ornamental canna that most SW Florida gardeners are familiar with. It is less showy than some ornamental canna varieties but far superior ecologically — it is native, it supports native butterflies as a host plant, and the large yellow flowers in July-October are genuinely attractive. Plant it where ornamental canna would go near water, but choose this one for its ecological value.
plants.fun_fact: Golden canna (Canna flaccida) was the original wild canna species that 18th and 19th century European plant breeders used to develop the hundreds of ornamental canna varieties now available worldwide. The large showy ornamental cannas in every garden center are all derived from this and related wild species. The breeders successfully increased flower size, improved color variety, and reduced seed production — but in doing so, reduced the ecological value.
plants.traditional_uses: The Calusa and Seminole harvested the starchy rhizomes of native canna species as a food source — similar to the edible rhizomes of the cultivated Asian canna (Canna indica). The starchy rhizome was boiled and eaten or processed into a starch similar to arrowroot.
